extraction_notes.note: The algorithm2e floats use \renewcommand{\nl}{...} and \tcc comments, so the parsed pseudocode lines lump caption, data and several statements; algorithm_step nodes were segmented by hand (one per operation) instead of from pseudocode_steps.
The research questions [Q1]-[Q6] are typed open_problem (questions open before the paper) with resolves edges to the results that answer them; they could also be read as mere motivation.
A remark environment that states a cited result (Wainwright 2009: Gaussian designs satisfy the Irrepresentable Condition w.h.p.) was retyped as an external theorem.
Theorem (equivalence of the three LARS formulations) has no proof environment; its proof is the derivation in Sections 5.3, 5.4 and the end of 6.2, emitted as three proof parts.
One sentence both defines the frozen next knot and asserts identity (3.4) proven later; kept as one definition node since a sentence cannot be split.
The notation tables of Section 1.6.3, the outline, the dependency diagram (omitted from the source) and the simulation set-up descriptions of Section 4 were not extracted as nodes.
Simulation findings read off figures are emitted as claims with rigor numerical.

nodes.name: Gaussian linear model
nodes.statement_short: High-dimensional Gaussian linear model $Y=X\beta^0+\eta$ with noise level $\sigma$ and design $X$ of rank $r$.
nodes.statement:
We denote by~$Y\in\mathbb R^n$ the response variable and we assume that
\begin{equation} Y=X\beta^0+\eta\sim\mathcal N_n(X\beta^0,\sigma^2 \mathrm{Id}_n),
\end{equation}
where~$\eta\sim\mathcal N_n(0,\sigma^2 \mathrm{Id}_n)$ is a Gaussian noise, the noise level~$\sigma>0$ may be known or may have to be estimated (depending on the context), and~$X\in\mathds R^{n\times p}$ has rank~$r>0$.

nodes.name: Justification of the knots in the noiseless identity design
nodes.statement_short: LASSO and LARS share knots for identity design; LASSO is the $\ell_1$ proximal operator at $\beta^0$.
nodes.statement: In this case, LASSO and LARS give the same knots~$\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots$  and the estimate of the LASSO is the outcome of the proximal operator of the~$\ell_1$-norm at point~$\beta^0\in\mathds R^p$, see for instance~\cite[Chapter 2]{hastie2015statistical}.

conclusions: \lambda_k=\beta^0_{(k)},
nodes.statement_short: With identity design and no noise, the LARS knots are the ordered entries of the target $\beta^0$.
nodes.statement:

\begin{equation} \lambda_k=\beta^0_{(k)},
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Selection event
nodes.statement_short: The selection event $\mathcal E$: the first $K$ signed variables entering LARS and the knot $\lambda_{K+1}$.
nodes.statement:
Working with the so-called `Irrepresentable Check' Condition\footnote{See Section~\ref{sec:Assumption} for a definition and detailed comments on this assumption.}~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, which can be efficiently checked in practice, we are able to provide the joint law of the LAR's knots conditional on the so-called `selection event' defined by
 \[
 \mathcal E:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =\imath_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=\imath_{K},\lambda_{K+1}\big\}.
 \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Joint law of LARS knots in Post-Selection Inference

nodes.name: Conditional Joint Law of the LARS knots
assumptions: Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots of the LARS and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}
conclusions:
conditional on the selection event~$\{\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$, the vector~$(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ obeys a law with the following density~(w.r.t. Lebesgue measure) 
\[
{\mathrm Q}^{-1}_{(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1})}
\,
\Big(
\prod_{k=1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)
\Big)
\,
\mathds{1}_{\{\ell_1\geq \ell_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\ell_{K}\geq\lambda_{K+1}\}}\text{ at point }(\ell_1, \ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{K}),
nodes.statement_short: Under Irrepresentable Check, conditional on the selection event, the first $K$ LARS knots have a truncated product-Gaussian (Gaussian order statistics mixture) density.
nodes.statement:
Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots of the LARS and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, then, conditional on the selection event~$\{\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$, the vector~$(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ obeys a law with the following density~(w.r.t. Lebesgue measure) 
\[
{\mathrm Q}^{-1}_{(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1})}
\,
\Big(
\prod_{k=1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)
\Big)
\,
\mathds{1}_{\{\ell_1\geq \ell_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\ell_{K}\geq\lambda_{K+1}\}}\text{ at point }(\ell_1, \ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{K}),
\]
where~${\mathrm Q}_{(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1})}$ is a normalizing constant,~$\varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}$ is the standard Gaussian density with mean~$m_k$ and variance~$v_k^2:=\sigma^2\rho_k^2$, are explicitly given by~\eqref{eq:def_mu_proj} and~\eqref{eq:def_rho}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Joint law of LARS knots in Post-Selection Inference
nodes.label: thm:Main1

nodes.name: Correlated target mu-bar
nodes.statement: Now, let us describe the dependency between~$(m_k,\rho_k^2)$ and~$\overline\mu^0:=X^\top X\beta^0$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Joint law of LARS knots in Post-Selection Inference

nodes.name: Dependence of the means and variances of the knots on the target
conclusions: m_k = c_k \, \varepsilon_k\, \langle X_{\overline\imath_k},P_{k-1}^\perp(X\beta^0)\rangle\quad \text{and}\quad \rho_k^2 =d_k\, \sin \measuredangle (X_{\overline\imath_k}, H_{k-1}),
nodes.statement_short: $m_k$ is proportional to the correlation of $X_{\overline\imath_k}$ with the residual of $X\beta^0$; $\rho_k^2$ to the sine of the angle with $H_{k-1}$.
nodes.statement:
By~\eqref{eq:def_mu_proj} and~\eqref{eq:def_rho}, one has 
\[
\forall k\in[K],\quad 
 m_k = c_k \, \varepsilon_k\, \langle X_{\overline\imath_k},P_{k-1}^\perp(X\beta^0)\rangle\quad \text{and}\quad \rho_k^2 =d_k\, \sin \measuredangle (X_{\overline\imath_k}, H_{k-1}),
\]
where~$c_k,d_k>0$ are constants that depends only on~$X_{\overline\imath_1},\ldots,X_{ \overline\imath_{k-1}}$,~$P_{k-1}^\perp$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto the orthogonal of~$H_{k-1}$,~$\varepsilon_k$ is the sign of the~$k^{\text{th}}$ variable entering the LARS path, and~$\measuredangle (X_{\overline\imath_k}, H_{k-1})$ is the angle between~$X_{\overline\imath_k}$ and~$H_{k-1}$.

\]

conclusions: namely, it is uniformly distributed over~$(0,1)$
nodes.statement_short: Under Irrepresentable Check, an admissible selection and $\mathds H_0: X\beta^0\in H_a$, the GSt p-value $\widehat\alpha_{abc}$ is exactly uniform.
nodes.statement:
Let~$a, b,$ and $c$ be such that~$0\leq a<b<c\leq K+1$.
Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} and~$\widehat m$ is chosen according to a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}}, then under the null hypothesis
\[
\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘‘}X\beta^0\in H_{a}\,\text{''},
\] 
and conditional on the selection event~$\big\{\,\widehat m\leq a\big\}$, it follows that
\begin{equation} \widehat\alpha_{abc}=\widehat\alpha_{abc}(\lambda_a,\lambda_b,\lambda_c, \widehat \imath_{1}, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{c-1}):=1-\frac{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)}{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1),
\end{equation}
namely, it is uniformly distributed over~$(0,1)$.

differentia: rejects if the~$p$-value~$\widehat\alpha_{abc}$ is less than the level~$\alpha$ of the test
nodes.statement:
We consider the following Generalized Spacing test procedures (GSt):
\begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_{abc}:=\mathds1_{\{\widehat\alpha_{abc}\leq\alpha\}},
\end{equation}
that rejects if the~$p$-value~$\widehat\alpha_{abc}$ is less than the level~$\alpha$ of the test.

assumptions: Let~$a, b,$ and $c$ be such that~$0\leq a<b<c\leq K+1$.

nodes.statement_short: With unknown variance, the studentized GtSt p-value $\widehat\beta_{abc}$ built on $\Lambda_k=\lambda_k/\widehat\sigma$ is exactly uniform under the null.
nodes.statement:
Let~$a, b,$ and $c$ be such that~$0\leq a<b<c\leq K+1$.
Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} and~$\widehat m$ is chosen according to a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}} then under the null hypothesis
\[
\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{a}\,\text{'},
\] 
and conditional on the selection event~$\big\{\widehat m \leq a\big\}$, it follows that
\[
 \widehat  \beta_{abc}= \widehat  \beta_{abc}( {\Lambda_a},{ \Lambda_b},{ \Lambda_c}, \widehat \imath_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}):= 1 - 
  \frac{\widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_b)}
 {\widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_a)}\sim \mathcal{U}(0,1),
\]
where $\Lambda_k:=\lambda_k/\widehat\sigma$.

nodes.statement:
Assume that the design~$X$ is orthogonal, namely~$X^\top X=\mathrm{Id}_{p}$.
Let~$a_0$ be an integer such that~$0\leq a_0\leq K-1$.
If~$\widehat m$ is chosen according to a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}}, then under the null hypothesis
\[
\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{a_0}\,\text{'},
\] 
and conditional on the selection event~$\big\{\widehat m=a_0\big\}$, it follows that the test~$\mathcal{S}_{a_0,a_0+1,K+1}$ is uniformly more powerful than any of the tests~$ \mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ for~$a_0\leq a <b<c \leq K+1$.

More precisely, in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:zazPower}, it is shown that 
\[

for orthogonal designs, where~$\preccurlyeq$ denotes stochastic ordering.

\widehat\imath_k:=\overline \imath_k+p\,\Big(\frac{1-\varepsilon_k}2\Big)\in[2p],

nodes.statement_short: Signed variable $\widehat\imath_k=\overline\imath_k+p(1-\varepsilon_k)/2\in[2p]$ encodes both the entering variable and its sign.
nodes.statement:
We denote by~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_k)\in[2p]^k$ the `signed}' variables that enter the model along the~LARS path with the convention that
\begin{equation} \widehat \imath_k:=\overline \imath_k+p\,\Big(\frac{1-\varepsilon_k}2\Big),
\end{equation}
so that~$\widehat \imath_k\in[2p]$ is a useful way of encoding both the variable~$\overline \imath_k\in[p]$ and its sign~$\varepsilon_k=\pm1$ as used in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR3}.

nodes.name: Correlation vector
nodes.statement: We denote by~$\overline Z:=X^\top Y$ the {\it correlation} vector such that~$\overline Z_k$ is the scalar product between the~$k^{\text{th}}$ predictor and the response variable, and we denote by~$\sigma^2\overline R$ its variance-covariance matrix.

nodes.name: Symmetrized correlation vector, its mean and covariance
nodes.statement_short: $Z=(\overline Z,-\overline Z)$ with mean $\mu^0=(\overline\mu^0,-\overline\mu^0)$ and covariance $\sigma^2R$, $R$ the block matrix built from $X^\top X$.
nodes.statement:
For the sake of presentation, we may consider the~$2p$-vector
\begin{equation} Z:=(\overline Z,-\overline Z)=(X^\top Y ,-X^\top Y ),
\end{equation}
whose mean is given by
\begin{equation} \mu^0:=(\overline R\beta^0,-\overline R\beta^0)=(X^\top X\beta^0,-X^\top X\beta^0)=(\overline\mu^0,-\overline\mu^0),
\end{equation}
and whose variance-covariance matrix is~$\sigma^2 R$ with 
\begin{equation} R
=\left[\begin{array}{cc} \overline R & -\overline R \\-\overline R & \overline R\end{array}\right]
=\left[\begin{array}{cc} X^\top X & -X^\top X \\-X^\top X & X^\top X\end{array}\right].
\end{equation}

nodes.statement: Z:=(\overline Z,-\overline Z)=(X^\top Y ,-X^\top Y ),

nodes.name: Selective testing framework
nodes.statement:
The testing procedures under consideration are not standard since the~$(H_{a})_{a=1}^{K}$ are random subspaces.
We are interested in the framework of selective testing, namely, testing procedures conditional on the selection event~$\{\widehat m=a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}\}$, for some fixed~$a\in[K-1]$.
Conditional on the event, note that~$H_{a}$ is fixed.
By convention, we may consider the case~$a=0$, that is, testing the global null hypothesis.

nodes.statement:
We define the set of {\it Active Sets}~$\mathcal{A}_K$ as all the  sequences~$i_1,\ldots,i_K$ of signed variables such that~$j_1,\ldots,j_K$ are pairwise different, where the~$j$'s are defined by~\eqref{e:findices}, namely 
\[
\mathcal{A}_K:=\big\{(i_1,\ldots,i_K)\in[2p]^K\ :\ j_1,\ldots,  j_K\text{ are pairwise different}\big\}.
\]

nodes.name: Gaussian designs satisfy the Irrepresentable Condition w.h.p.
assumptions: a design matrix~$X\in\mathds{R}^{n\times p}$ whose rows are drawn independently with respect to a centered Gaussian distribution with variance-covariance matrix satisfying~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} (for instance the identity matrix)
when~$n\gtrsim K\log(p-K)$
conclusions: satisfies~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} with high probability
nodes.statement_short: Random designs with i.i.d. Gaussian rows whose covariance satisfies the condition satisfy it w.h.p. once $n\gtrsim K\log(p-K)$.
nodes.statement:
This condition has been intensively studied in the literature and it is now well established that some random matrix models satisfy it with high probability.
For instance, one may refer to~\cite{wainwright2009sharp}, where it is shown that a design matrix~$X\in\mathds{R}^{n\times p}$ whose rows are drawn independently with respect to a centered Gaussian distribution with variance-covariance matrix satisfying~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} (for instance the identity matrix) satisfies~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} with high probability when~$n\gtrsim K\log(p-K)$, where~$ \gtrsim$ denotes an inequality up to some multiplicative constant.

nodes.name: Law of the maximal order of Irrepresentable Check for Gaussian designs
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo study: for $p=1000$, Irrepresentable Check holds up to $K_{\max}\approx0.16n$ ($n=100$) or $0.12n$ ($n=500$).
nodes.statement:
Taking the (signed) variables entering the model with LARS in an iid Gaussian design and as response variable a centered Gaussian vector with iid entries from~$10,000$ Monte Carlo repetitions, Figure~\ref{fig:F1} illustrates the law of the maximal order~$K_{\mathrm{max}}$ for which the Irrepresentable Check condition holds.
For example, we found that for~$p=1,000$ and~$n=100$~$($with ratio~$n/p=0.1)$ resp.~$n=500$~$($with ratio~$n/p=0.5)$, the Irrepresentable Check condition~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} of order~$K_{\mathrm{max}}$ holds when~$K_{\mathrm{max}}$ is about~$K_{\mathrm{max}}\simeq 0.16\times n=16$ respectively~$K_{\mathrm{max}}\simeq 0.12\times n=60$, see Figure~\ref{fig:F1}.

where~$(1, \ldots, 1)$ is the column vector of size~$k$ whose entries are equal to one;~$\sigma^2M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}$ is the variance-covariance matrix of the vector~$ (Z_{i_1}, \cdots , Z_{i_{k}})$
and~$(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k}})$ is a row vector of size~$k$.

nodes.name: Equivalent formulation of the Irrepresentable Condition
assumptions: Let~$X$ and~$R$ be defined by~\eqref{eq:white}.
conclusions:
Furthermore, they imply that for all~$(i_1,\ldots,i_{K})\in\mathcal A_K$ one has
\begin{equation}
\notag
\max\Big[
\max_{{j\neq i_1}}\theta_j(\imath_1),\,\ldots,\max_{j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}\theta_j(i_1,\ldots,i_{K})\Big]<1
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalent formulation of the Irrepresentable Condition
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\theta_j$ via sign matrices to get $X_j^\top X_S(X_S^\top X_S)^{-1}\overline v$, then maximize over sign vectors.
nodes.statement:
Let~$S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_k\}\subset[p]$ and~$j\in[2p]\setminus S$.
Let~$\overline v=(\overline v_1,\ldots,\overline v_k)\in\{-1,1\}^k$ and define~$i_\ell = j_\ell+p(1-\overline v_\ell)/2$ for~$\ell\in[k]$.
Note that
\begin{align*}
\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_k) &= \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}  
(1, \ldots, 1)\\
&= \Big[X_j^\top X_S\mathrm{Diag}(\overline v)\Big]M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}(1, \ldots, 1)\\
&=\Big[  X_j^\top X_S\mathrm{Diag}(\overline v)\Big]M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}\Big[\mathrm{Diag}(\overline v)\overline v\Big]\\
&= X_j^\top X_S\Big[\mathrm{Diag}(\overline v)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}\mathrm{Diag}(\overline v)\Big]\overline v\\
&= X_j^\top X_S\big( X_S^\top  X_S\big)^{-1}\overline v.
\end{align*}
Now, observe that 
\[
\max_{||v||_\infty\leq1}v^\top\big( X_S^\top  X_S\big)^{-1} X_S^\top X_j
=\max_{\overline v\in\{-1,1\}^k} X_j^\top X_S\big( X_S^\top  X_S\big)^{-1}\overline v,
\]
showing the equivalence between the two assumptions.

nodes.name: Fix support and signs
nodes.statement_short: Fix a support, an index and a sign vector.
nodes.statement:
Let~$S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_k\}\subset[p]$ and~$j\in[2p]\setminus S$.
Let~$\overline v=(\overline v_1,\ldots,\overline v_k)\in\{-1,1\}^k$ and define~$i_\ell = j_\ell+p(1-\overline v_\ell)/2$ for~$\ell\in[k]$.

nodes.name: Rewrite theta
nodes.statement_short: Express $\theta_j$ as $X_j^\top X_S(X_S^\top X_S)^{-1}\overline v$.

nodes.name: Conclude equivalence
nodes.statement_short: Maximum over the $\ell_\infty$ ball equals maximum over sign vectors.
nodes.statement:
Now, observe that 
\[
\max_{||v||_\infty\leq1}v^\top\big( X_S^\top  X_S\big)^{-1} X_S^\top X_j
=\max_{\overline v\in\{-1,1\}^k} X_j^\top X_S\big( X_S^\top  X_S\big)^{-1}\overline v,
\]
showing the equivalence between the two assumptions.

nodes.name: Irrepresentable Condition of order 1 under normalization
nodes.statement:
One may require that the design be `normalized' so that~$R_{i,i}=1$, namely its columns have unit Euclidean norm.
Under this normalization, one can check that~$R$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} of order~$K=1$.
Hence, up to some normalization, one can always assume~\eqref{eq:Irr_matrix} of order~$K=1$.

nodes.name: Irrepresentable Check witnessed along the LARS path
nodes.statement:
When computing the LARS path, one has to compute the values 
\[
X_j^\top X_{\overline S^{k}}\big( X_{\overline S^{k}}^\top  X_{\overline S^{k}}\big)^{-1}\varepsilon^{k},
\] 
see for instance Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} or Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR2}, where these values are given by~$\theta$, as shown by Proposition~\ref{prop:Irrepresentable}.
This implies that, in practice, along the LARS path, one witnesses the maximal order~$K$ for which Irrepresentable Check~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} holds.

nodes.name: Projection onto the orthogonal of the putative selected span
nodes.statement: Let~$P^\perp_{K}$ be the orthogonal projection on the orthogonal to~$H_K^{j_1,\ldots, j_{K}}:=\mathrm{Span}(X_{j_1}, \ldots, X_{ j_{K}})$.

nodes.name: Variance estimator for putative indices
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat\sigma^{j_1,\ldots,j_K}=\|P_K^\perp Y\|_2/\sqrt{n-K}$, residual norm after projecting out the putative support.
nodes.statement:
We define   
 \begin{equation} \widehat \sigma^{j_1,\ldots, j_{K}}  := \frac{ ||P^\perp_{K} Y||_2 }{\sqrt{n-K}} .
    \end{equation}
   By a slight abuse of notation, we can index the estimator above by the signed indexes~$i_1, \ldots, i_{K}$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.15)
nodes.statement: \widehat \sigma^{j_1,\ldots, j_{K}}  := \frac{ ||P^\perp_{K} Y||_2 }{\sqrt{n-K}} .
nodes.label: e:def_sigmas

nodes.name: Estimator of the noise level
nodes.statement:
Eventually, we set 
\[
    \widehat \sigma  := \widehat \sigma^{\,\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{K}},
\]
 the estimates of the standard deviation~$\sigma$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.16)
nodes.statement: \widehat S =\big \{\overline  \imath_1,\overline  \imath_2,\ldots,\overline \imath_{\widehat m}\big\}.
nodes.label: e:selection_procedure

nodes.name: Stopping Rule (admissible selection procedure)
nodes.statement_short: The selected size $\widehat m$ is a stopping time: $\{\widehat m\le a\}$ depends only on $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_a$ and the entering variables.

nodes.name: Equation (2.17)
nodes.statement: \tag{$\bf\mathcal A_{\mathrm{\,Stop}}$} \mathds 1_{\{\widehat m\leq a\}}\text{~is a measurable function of~}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_a, \widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{K})\,.
nodes.label: e:stopping_rule

nodes.name: A decision rule violating the Stopping Rule
nodes.statement_short: Choosing between 1- and 2-sparse by thresholding $\lambda_2$ is not admissible, since it can only select sizes at least 2.
nodes.statement:
We now give an example to show that {\eqref{e:stopping_rule}} implies some restriction.
Suppose, for example, that we want to decide wether the target~$\beta^0$ is two sparse or one sparse.
A natural decision rule is to look at large values of the second knot~$\lambda_2$, if~$\text{‘‘}\,\lambda_2 > \mathrm{(some\ threshold)}\text{''}$   choose~$ m=2$  otherwise choose~$m=1$.
  This rule does not satisfy~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}, since looking at~$\lambda_2$  we can choose only sizes~$m$ greater than or equal to 2.

nodes.name: Orthogonal projections onto the selected subspaces
nodes.statement: Denote by~$P_k(Y)$ (resp.~$P^\perp_k(Y)$) the orthogonal projection of the observation~$Y$ onto~$H_k$ (resp. the orthogonal of~$H_k$) for all~$k\geq 1$ where~$H_k$ are defined by~\eqref{eq:sequence_subspaces}.

nodes.name: Projection-based selection procedures are admissible
assumptions: $h$ any measurable function
conclusions: determines a class of selection procedures satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}
nodes.statement:
Given $h$ any measurable function, 
\[
\mathds 1_{\{\widehat m\leq a\}}=h(P_a(Y)),
\]
determines a class of selection procedures satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}.

nodes.name: Testing for false negatives after model selection
nodes.statement_short: Test at exact level $\alpha$ that the selected model contains the true support, i.e. $X\beta^0\in H_{\widehat m}$ (no false negatives).
nodes.statement:
Once one has selected a model of size~$\widehat m$, one may be willing to test if~$\widehat S$ contains the true support~$S^0$ by considering the null hypothesis 
\[
\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘}S^0\subseteq \widehat S\,\text{'},
\] 
namely there are no false negatives.
Equivalently, one aims at testing the null hypothesis
\begin{equation} \mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘}X\beta^0\in H_{\widehat m}\,\text{'},
\end{equation}
at an exact significance level~$\alpha\in(0,1)$, where~$(H_a)_{a=0}^{K-1}$ is defined by~\eqref{eq:sequence_subspaces}.

nodes.name: Equation (2.18)
nodes.statement: \mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘}X\beta^0\in H_{\widehat m}\,\text{'},
nodes.label: e:nullH

nodes.name: Frozen residual and regression Pi
nodes.statement_short: Frozen residual $Z^{(i_1..i_k)}_j=(Z_j-\Pi_{i_1..i_k}(Z_j))/(1-\theta_j)$, $\Pi$ the regression of $Z_j$ on $Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_k}$.
nodes.statement:
Given~$K$ as defined in~\eqref{e:K} and fixed~$i_1,\ldots, i_{K+1}\in[2p]$, one may define
\begin{equation} \forall j \text{ s.t. } \theta_j(i_1, \ldots, i_{k})\neq1,\quad 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j:=\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation} \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j) :=  \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}  (Z_{i_1}, \ldots, Z_{i_{k}})
\end{equation}
and~$\theta_j(i_1, \ldots, i_{k})$ is given by~\eqref{eq:thetai}.

nodes.name: Equation (3.1)
nodes.statement:
\forall j \text{ s.t. } \theta_j(i_1, \ldots, i_{k})\neq1,\quad 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j:=\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})},
nodes.label: e:frozenZ

nodes.name: Equation (3.2)
nodes.statement: \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j) :=  \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}  (Z_{i_1}, \ldots, Z_{i_{k}})
nodes.label: e:Pi

nodes.name: Frozen next knot lambda^(i)
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda^{(i_1..i_k)}_{k+1}$ is the max of the frozen residuals; it equals $\lambda_{k+1}$ on the event that the first signed variables are $i_1..i_k$.
nodes.statement:
From this point on, we introduce
\begin{equation} \forall k\geq 0,\quad
\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}:=\max_{j: \theta_j(i_1, \ldots, i_{k})<1}Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j,
\end{equation}

\[
\sum_{(i_1,\ldots,i_{K})\in\mathcal{A}_{K}}\mathds 1_{\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}\}}=1\quad\text{almost\ surely}.

nodes.name: Proposition as a polyhedral lemma for multiple linear statistics
nodes.statement_short: The characterization of the selection event extends the polyhedral lemma of selective inference to several linear statistics.
nodes.statement:
{\bf Is Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} a new polyhedral lemma?}
The characterization of the selection event for the inference of a single testing statistic has been known as the ‘polyhedral lemma' in the literature, see for instance \cite[Figure~6.9]{hastie2015statistical} and references therein. This result is the cornerstone of selective inference with sparse models. It is based on two ingredients: First, the selection event can be expressed as a polyhedra; Second, conditional on the selection event, any linear statistics is distributed according to a truncated Gaussian with independent truncation bounds. 

A first remark is that the polyhedral lemma is shown for one linear statistic and, as far as we known, there is no polyhedral lemma for multiple linear statistics. The interesting point is that our result (Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur}) can be seen as a polyhedral lemma for multiple linear statistics. Under \eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, the selection event $\{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K\}$ corresponds to a polyhedra described by the $Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\cdots, i_{k-1})}$ variables in the third point of Proposition \ref{prop:reccur}. Our main result shows that the joint law of these multiple linear statistics are the Gaussian distribution restricted to the polyhedra $\{\ell_1\geq\ldots\geq \ell_K\geq\lambda_{K+1}\}$, see Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1}.

Note that the selection event has to include $\lambda_{K+1}$. As discussed above, our polyhedral lemma (Theorem \ref{thm:Main1} and Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur}) shows that, conditional on the selection event, $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K$ are distributed with respect to a Gaussian distribution restricted to the polyhedra $\{\ell_1\geq\ldots\geq \ell_K\geq\lambda_{K+1}\}$. If one does not include $\lambda_{K+1}$ in the selection event, then one has to integrate this latter conditional law with respect to the distribution of $\lambda_{K+1}$ which is not known.

nodes.name: Proof of the Conditional Joint Law of the LARS knots
nodes.statement_short: Frozen knots are independent Gaussians; on the selection event they equal the knots and the event is their ordering, giving the truncated density.
nodes.statement:
From the definition of the Gaussian random variable~$ Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}~$ in~\eqref{e:frozenZ} one can deduce that its mean~$m_k$ is given by~\eqref{eq:def_mu_proj} and its standard deviation~$v_k$ by~\eqref{eq:def_rho}, considering putative indices for the selected variables. By the second point of Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur}, we know that these variables are independent.
We deduce that their joint density~$(Z_{i_1}, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, \ldots, Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})})$ is 
\[
\prod_{k=1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k),
\]
 with respect to Lebesgue measure.
For now on, we condition on  $\mathcal E:=\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_{K+1}\}$ and we assume that~$(i_1,\ldots, i_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}. By the first equality of the third point of Proposition \ref{prop:reccur} we known that~$\mathcal E=\big\{\lambda_{K+1}\leq Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})} \leq  \cdots \leq Z_{i_1}\big\}$, and on the event~$\mathcal E$,
\begin{equation} (Z_{i_1}, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, \ldots, Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})})
=
(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_K).
\end{equation}
Conditional on~$\mathcal E$, the joint density of~$(Z_{i_1}, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, \ldots, Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})})$ is proportional to
\begin{equation} \Big(
\prod_{k=1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)
\Big)
\,
\mathds{1}_{\{\ell_1\geq \ell_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\ell_{K}\geq\lambda_{K+1}\}},
\end{equation}
 with respect to Lebesgue measure, and by~\eqref{e:equal} it is the conditional density of the knots.

nodes.statement:
On the numerical side, note that this quantity can be computed using {\it Quasi Monte Carlo} (QMC) methods as in~\cite[Chapter 5.1]{genz2009computation} or Appendix~\ref{app:cbc}.
The function~$\mathds{F}_{abc}$ gives the CDF of~$\lambda_b$ conditional on~$\lambda_a,\lambda_c$ and on some selection event, as shown in the next proposition.

If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} and~$\widehat m$ is chosen according to a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}}, then under the null hypothesis

nodes.name: Deterministic model size is admissible
nodes.statement_short: A fixed $\widehat m=a$ satisfies the stopping rule, so the conditional CDF holds for every $a<b<c$.
nodes.statement:
Note that the deterministic choice~$\widehat m=a$, for a fixed~$a\in[K-1]$, is a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}} and Proposition \ref{prop:fabc} holds.
This shows that if~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, then, under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘‘}X\beta^0\in H_{a}\,\text{''}$,

\end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of exact level of the Generalized Spacing test
nodes.statement_short: Probability integral transform of the conditional CDF of $\lambda_b$; take the complement to get a p-value.
nodes.statement:
From Proposition \ref{prop:fabc} we know that under~$\mathds H_0$ and conditional on the selection event~$\big\{\widehat m=a\big\}$, Eq.~\eqref{eqFabc} gives the conditional CDF of~$\lambda_b$.
As a consequence, 
  \[
  \frac{
  \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)    }{    \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)  }  \sim  \mathcal  U(0,1).
  \]
  Finally, considerations of the distribution under the alternative  show that to obtain a~$p$-value, we must consider the complement to 1 of  the quantity above.

nodes.name: Spacing test and conservative spacing test as special cases
nodes.statement_short: With $b=a+1$, $c=a+2$ the GSt p-value reduces to the conservative spacing test of Taylor et al.
nodes.statement:
If one takes~$a=0$,~$b=1$, and~$c=2$ then
\[
\widehat\alpha_{012}=1-\frac{\Phi_{1}(\lambda_1)-\Phi_{1}(\lambda_2)}{\Phi_{1}(\lambda_0)-\Phi_{1}(\lambda_2)}
=\frac{1-\Phi_{1}(\lambda_1)}{1-\Phi_{1}(\lambda_2)}.
\]
Similarly, taking~$b=a+1$ and~$c=a+2$,
\[
\widehat\alpha_{a(a+1)(a+2)}
=\frac
{\Phi_{{a+1}}(\lambda_{a+1})-\Phi_{{a+1}}(\lambda_a)}
{\Phi_{{a+1}}(\lambda_{a+2})-\Phi_{{a+1}}(\lambda_a)}.
\]
which is the {\it conservative spacing test}, see \cite[Theorem~2]{taylor2014exact}.

assumptions: Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.

\]
nodes.statement_short: The p-value $\widehat\alpha_{\widehat m(\widehat m+1)(K+1)}$ is exactly uniform under the no-false-negative null, unconditionally on $\widehat m$.
nodes.statement:
Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath} and~$\widehat m$ is chosen according to a procedure satisfying~{\eqref{e:stopping_rule}}, then, conditional on the null hypothesis
\[
\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{‘‘}X\beta^0\in H_{\widehat m}\,\text{''},
\] 
it holds that
\[
\widehat\alpha_{\widehat m(\widehat m+1)(K+1)}:=1
-\frac{\mathds{F}_{\widehat m(\widehat m+1)(K+1)}(\lambda_{\widehat m+1})}{\mathds{F}_{\widehat m(\widehat m+1)(K+1)}(\lambda_{\widehat m})}
\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1),
\]
that is, it is uniformly distributed over~$(0,1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the exact false negative test
nodes.statement_short: Apply the GSt theorem with $b=a+1$, $c=K+1$; the uniform law does not depend on $a$, so de-condition on $\widehat m$.
nodes.statement:
By Theorem \ref{nt:pvalue}, the conditional law of~$\widehat\alpha_{a(a+1)(K+1)}$ with respect to~$\{\widehat m\leq a\}$ is the uniform distribution.
Note that the conditional law~\eqref{zaza5} does not depend on~$a,b=a+1,c=K+1$, hence this law is unconditional on~$\widehat m$.

nodes.name: Independence of the knots and the variance estimator
assumptions: Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots of LARS and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}
conclusions: conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$, the random variables~$( \lambda _1,\ldots,  \lambda_{K})$ and $\widehat \sigma$ are independent;

conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K\}$ and under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{K}\text{'}$, the random variables~$(\lambda_{K+1}/\widehat\sigma)$ and $\widehat \sigma$ are independent;

conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$ and under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{K}\text{'}$, the distribution of~$ (\lambda _1,\ldots, \lambda_{K})$ is given by Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1}, while the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma/\sigma$ is the same as the random variable
\[
(n-K)^{-\frac12}\,\Big({{\,\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-K}w_\ell^2}}\Big)^{\frac12}\,,
\]
where $W:=(w_1,\ldots,w_{n-K})$ is a ‘truncated' standard Gaussian vector with the truncation given by
\[
\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\lambda_{K+1}/\sigma\,,
\]
where $U\in\mathds R^{n\times (n-K)}$ is any matrix such that $UU^\top=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)}$, $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K))_{j\in[p]}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$.

nodes.statement:
Let~$(\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_K,\lambda_{K+1})$ be the first knots of LARS and let~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ be the first variables entering along the~LARS path.
If~$(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, then  
\begin{itemize}
\item conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$, the random variables~$( \lambda _1,\ldots,  \lambda_{K})$ and $\widehat \sigma$ are independent;
\item conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K\}$ and under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{K}\text{'}$, the random variables~$(\lambda_{K+1}/\widehat\sigma)$ and $\widehat \sigma$ are independent;
\item conditional on $\{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$ and under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{K}\text{'}$, the distribution of~$ (\lambda _1,\ldots, \lambda_{K})$ is given by Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1}, while the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma/\sigma$ is the same as the random variable
\[
(n-K)^{-\frac12}\,\Big({{\,\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-K}w_\ell^2}}\Big)^{\frac12}\,,
\]
where $W:=(w_1,\ldots,w_{n-K})$ is a ‘truncated' standard Gaussian vector with the truncation given by
\[
\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\lambda_{K+1}/\sigma\,,
\]
where $U\in\mathds R^{n\times (n-K)}$ is any matrix such that $UU^\top=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K)}$, $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K))_{j\in[p]}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$.
\end{itemize}

nodes.name: Centering of the residual under the null
nodes.statement:
Under the null hypothesis $\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{K}\text{'}$, the Gaussian vectors~$P_{K}^\perp(Y)$~$($see~\eqref{e:def_sigmas}$)$, defining the variance estimate~$\widehat \sigma^2$, is centered. This null hypothesis means that the true support is included in the set of the~$K$ first indices chosen by LARS.
One may choose~$K$ large enough to guarantee this null hypothesis.

nodes.name: Multivariate t density
nodes.statement:
Recall that, up to some positive numerical constant, the probability density function of the multivariate~$t$-distribution with~$(n-K)$ degrees of freedom, mean~$m=(m_1,\ldots,m_K)$ and variance-covariance matrix $\mathrm{Diag}(\rho_1^2,\ldots,\rho_K^2)$ is given by
\[
\widetilde\varphi(t_1,\ldots,t_K):=
\Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\sum_{k=1}^K \Big(\frac{t_k-m_k}{\rho_k}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{n}2}.
\]

nodes.name: Proof of the Conditional Joint Law of the Studentized LARS knots
nodes.statement_short: Frozen knots are independent Gaussians independent of $\widehat\sigma$, so their ratios are multivariate $t$; the selection event is their ordering.
nodes.statement:
Let us fix some values~$i_1, \ldots, i_{K}$. From the definition of the Gaussian random variable~$ Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}~$ in~\eqref{e:frozenZ}, one can deduce that its mean~$m_k$ is given by~\eqref{eq:def_mu_proj} and its standard deviation~$v_k:=\sigma\rho_k$ by~\eqref{eq:def_rho}, considering putative indices for the selected variables. By the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:frozen}, we know that these variables are independent of~$\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$. We deduce that the vector~$(Z_{i_1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},\ldots,Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})$ has density a multivariate~$t$-distribution with~${n-K}$ degrees of freedom, mean~$m=(m_1,\ldots,m_K)$ and variance-covariance matrix~$\mathrm{Diag}(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_K)$. Furthermore, by~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas} of Proposition~\ref{p:frozen}, we know that this vector is independent of  $({Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j}/{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}})_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$, and, in particular, independent of $\Lambda_{K+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}:=\max_j\{{Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j}/{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}\}$. Recall that, conditional on 
 \[
 \mathcal E:=\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_{K+1}\},
 \] and assuming that~$(i_1,\ldots, i_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, Proposition \ref{prop:reccur} implies that 
 \[
 \mathcal E=\Bigg\{\Lambda_{K+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}\leq \frac{Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}}{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}} \leq  \cdots \leq \frac{Z_{i_1}}{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}\Bigg\}\,.
 \]
Furthermore, on the event~$\mathcal E$ we have
\begin{equation}
\notag
(Z_{i_1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},  \ldots, Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},\Lambda_{K+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})})
=
(\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_{K},\Lambda_{K+1}).
\end{equation}
Because of the independence above, this implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.name: Selection event
nodes.statement_short: The selection event is the ordering of the studentized frozen knots.
nodes.statement:
Recall that, conditional on 
 \[
 \mathcal E:=\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_{K+1}\},
 \] and assuming that~$(i_1,\ldots, i_K)$ satisfies~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath}, Proposition \ref{prop:reccur} implies that 
 \[
 \mathcal E=\Bigg\{\Lambda_{K+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}\leq \frac{Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}}{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}} \leq  \cdots \leq \frac{Z_{i_1}}{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}\Bigg\}\,.
 \]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: On the event the frozen ratios are the $\Lambda_k$; conclude.
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, on the event~$\mathcal E$ we have
\begin{equation}
\notag
(Z_{i_1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},  \ldots, Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},\Lambda_{K+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})})
=
(\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_{K},\Lambda_{K+1}).
\end{equation}
Because of the independence above, this implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.statement_short: $t$-analogues $\widetilde\varphi_{ab}$, $\widetilde{\mathcal I}_{ab}$ and the unnormalized conditional CDF $\widetilde{\mathds F}_{abc}$ of $\Lambda_b$.
nodes.statement:
For~$0\leq a<b\leq K+1$, we introduce 
 \begin{align}
 \notag
 \widetilde\varphi_{ab}(t_{a+1},\ldots,t_{b-1})
 &:=
\Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\sum_{k=a+1}^{b-1} \Big(\frac{t_k}{\rho_k}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{{n-K}+b-a}2}\\
\notag
\widetilde{\mathcal{I}}_{ab}(s,t)
&:=
\int_{\{s\geq t_{a+1}\geq \ldots \geq t_{b-1}\geq t\}}\widetilde\varphi_{ab}(t_{a+1},\ldots,t_{b-1})\mathrm d t_{a+1} \cdots \mathrm d t_{b-1},
 \end{align}
 with the convention~$\widetilde{\mathcal{I}}_{ab}(s,t)=1$ when~$b=a+1$: and also
\begin{align} \widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(t)
&:=
\mathds{1}_{\{\Lambda_c\leq t\leq \Lambda_a\}}
\displaystyle
\int\displaylimits_{\Lambda_{c}}^{t}
\widetilde{\mathcal{I}}_{ab}({\Lambda_a},\ell_b)\,\widetilde{\mathcal{I}}_{bc}(\ell_b,{\Lambda_c})\,
\Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\Big(\frac{\ell_b}{\rho_b}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{{n-K}+1}2}
\mathrm d\ell_b\\
\notag
&\text{for }0\leq a<b<c\leq K+1,\ t\in\mathds{R}.
\end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of exact level of the Generalized t-Spacing test
nodes.statement_short: Centered null plus the studentized joint law give a truncated $t$ density; admissibility makes $\{\widehat m=a\}$ independent, and integration yields the CDF.
nodes.statement:
Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}.
 From Proposition~\ref{prop:H0}, conditional on 
\[
 \mathcal F:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \Lambda_a,\Lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,
 \]
and under the null hypothesis~$\mathds H_0\,:\ \text{`}X\beta^0\in H_{a}\,\text{'}$, we know that~$m_{a+1}=\ldots=m_K=0$. From Theorem~\ref{thm:Main2} we know that the density of~$(\Lambda_{a+1},\Lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\Lambda_K)$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$ is given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \notag
    (const)  
    \Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\sum_{k=a+1}^K \Big(\frac{t_k}{\rho_k}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{{n}-a}2}
    \, \mathds{1}_{\Lambda_a \geq \ell_{a+1}\geq \cdots \geq \ell_K\geq  \Lambda_{K+1}}.
   \end{equation}

\noindent From the definition of assumption~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}, and on the event~$\mathcal F$, we know that the indicator~$\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is a measurable function of~$\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{a-1}$, which are respectively equal to $Z_{i_1},\ldots,  Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}$ on~$\mathcal F$ by~\eqref{e:frozen}. By \eqref{e:indep_sigmas} of Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur}, we deduce that $\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},\ldots,\lambda_K/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})$ and of $\Lambda_{K+1}:=\lambda_{K+1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event 
 \[
 \mathcal G:=\big\{\widehat m =a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \Lambda_a,\Lambda_{K+1}\big\}.
 \]
Now, a simple integration shows that  
\begin{equation} \mathds{P}\big[\Lambda_b\leq t\ |\ \widehat m =a,\Lambda_a,\Lambda_c, \widehat \imath_{1},\ldots,\widehat \imath_{K}\big]=\frac{\widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(t)}{\widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_a)}.
\end{equation}
As a consequence and under the same conditioning, one has
  \[
  \frac{
  \widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_b)    }{    \widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_a)  }  \sim  \mathcal  U(0,1).
  \]
  Finally, considerations of the distribution under the alternative  show that  to obtain a~$p$-value we must consider the complement to~$1$ of  the quantity above.

Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}.

By \eqref{e:indep_sigmas} of Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur}, we deduce that $\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}},\ldots,\lambda_K/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})$ and of $\Lambda_{K+1}:=\lambda_{K+1}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Probability integral transform and complement give the p-value.
nodes.statement:
As a consequence and under the same conditioning, one has
  \[
  \frac{
  \widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_b)    }{    \widetilde{\mathds{F}}_{abc}(\Lambda_a)  }  \sim  \mathcal  U(0,1).
  \]
  Finally, considerations of the distribution under the alternative  show that  to obtain a~$p$-value we must consider the complement to~$1$ of  the quantity above.

nodes.name: Generalized t-Spacing test (GtSt)
differentia: rejects if the~$p$-value~$\widehat\beta_{abc}$ is less than the level~$\alpha$ of the test
nodes.statement:
Consider the following testing procedures:
\begin{equation} \mathcal{T}_{abc}:=\mathds1_{\{\widehat\beta_{abc}\leq\alpha\}},
\end{equation}
that rejects if the~$p$-value~$\widehat\beta_{abc}$ is less than the level~$\alpha$ of the test.
This test statistic generalizes previous test statistics that appeared in~$t$-Spacing Tests, as presented in~\cite{azais2018power} for instance, and will be referred to as the {\it Generalized~$t$-Spacing test} (GtSt).

nodes.name: Equation (3.26)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{T}_{abc}:=\mathds1_{\{\widehat\beta_{abc}\leq\alpha\}},
nodes.label: zaza66

nodes.name: t-Spacing test as a special case
nodes.statement_short: With $b=a+1$, $c=a+2$ the GtSt p-value is the $t$-spacing test of Azais et al., with $\boldsymbol T_k$ a Student CDF.
nodes.statement:
If one takes~$a=0$,~$b=1$ and~$c=2$, then one gets
\[
\widehat\beta_{012}=1-\frac{\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_1)-\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_2)}{\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_0)-\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_2)}
=\frac{1-\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_1)}{1-\boldsymbol{T}_{1}(\Lambda_2)}.
\]
Similarly, taking~$b=a+1$ and~$c=a+2$, one gets
\[
\widehat\beta_{a(a+1)(a+2)}
=\frac
{\boldsymbol{T}_{{a+1}}(\Lambda_{a+1})-\boldsymbol{T}_{{a+1}}(\Lambda_a)}
{\boldsymbol{T}_{{a+1}}(\Lambda_{a+2})-\boldsymbol{T}_{{a+1}}(\Lambda_a)}.
\]
which is the {\it $t$-spacing test} as presented in~\cite{azais2018power}, where 
\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{T}_k(\ell):=\int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^\ell\Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\Big(\frac{\ell}{\rho_k}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{{n-K}+1}2}\mathrm d\ell
\end{equation}
is, up to some positive numerical constant, the CDF of a centered~$t$-Student distribution with variance~$\rho_k^2$ and~$n-K$ degrees of freedom.
nodes.label: rem:tST

nodes.name: Equation (3.27)
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol{T}_k(\ell):=\int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^\ell\Bigg[1+\frac1{n-K}{\Big(\frac{\ell}{\rho_k}\Big)^2}\Bigg]^{-\frac{{n-K}+1}2}\mathrm d\ell

nodes.statement: We write~$I_0$ of the set $I_0=\big\{k\in[K]\ :\ \mathds H_{0,k}\text{ is true}\big\}$.

nodes.name: False and true positives
nodes.statement: Given a subset~$\widehat R\subseteq [K]$ of hypotheses that we consider as rejected, we call {\it false positive} ($\mathrm{FP}$) and {\it true positive} ($\mathrm{TP}$) the quantities~$\mathrm{FP}=\mathrm{card}(\,\widehat R\cap I_0)$ and~$\mathrm{TP}=\mathrm{card}(\,\widehat R\setminus I_0)$.

nodes.statement_short: BH rejection set: reject all $k$ with $\widehat p_k\le\alpha\widehat k/K$, $\widehat k$ the largest $k$ with $\widehat p_{(k)}\le\alpha k/K$.

nodes.name: False Discovery Rate
nodes.statement:
Recall the definition of the FDR as the mean of the False Discovery Proportion ($\mathrm{FDP}$), namely
\[
\mathrm{FDR}:=\mathds E\Big[\underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TP}}\mathds 1_{\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TP}\geq1}}_{\mathrm{FDP}}\Big],
\]
where the expectation is unconditional on the sequence of variables entering the model, while the hypotheses that are being tested are conditional on the  sequence of variables entering the model.

nodes.name: Decomposition of the FDR over selected sequences
nodes.statement:
This FDR can be understood by invoking the following decomposition
\[
\mathrm{FDR}=\sum_{(\imath_1,\ldots,\imath_K)\in[p]^K}
\!\!\!\!\!\!
\overline\pi_{ (\imath_1,\ldots, \imath_K)}\,\mathds E\big[\mathrm{FDP}|\overline\imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\overline\imath_K=i_K\big],
\]
where~$\overline\pi_{ (\imath_1,\ldots, \imath_K)}=\mathds P\big\{\overline \imath_1=\imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K=\imath_K\big\}$.

nodes.name: LARS algorithm (standard formulation)
input: Correlations vector~$\overline Z$ and variance-covariance matrix~$\overline R$.
output: Sequence~$((\lambda_k,\overline \imath_k, \varepsilon_k))_{k\geq1}$ where~$\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\geq\ldots>0$ are the knots, and~$\overline \imath_1,\overline \imath_2,\ldots$ are the variables that enter the model with signs~$\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\ldots$~$(\varepsilon_k=\pm1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard LARS: start at the most correlated variable, move residual correlations along the equiangular direction until a new variable ties, and repeat.
nodes.statement:
\setcounter{AlgoLine}{0}
  \SetAlgoLined 
  
  \KwData{Correlations vector~$\overline Z$ and variance-covariance matrix~$\overline R$.} 
    
  \KwResult{Sequence~$((\lambda_k,\overline \imath_k, \varepsilon_k))_{k\geq1}$ where~$\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\geq\ldots>0$ are the knots, and~$\overline \imath_1,\overline \imath_2,\ldots$ are the variables that enter the model with signs~$\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\ldots$~$(\varepsilon_k=\pm1)$.}
    \BlankLine
    
    {\renewcommand{\nl}{\let\nl\nl} \tcc{Initialize computing~$(\lambda_1,\overline \imath_1,\varepsilon_1)$ and defining a ‘residual'~$\overline N^{(1)}$.}}
    Set~$k=1$,~$\displaystyle \lambda_1:=\max|\overline Z|$,~$\displaystyle \overline \imath_1:=\arg\max|\overline Z|$ and~$\varepsilon_1=\overline Z_{\overline \imath_1}/\lambda_1\in\pm1$, and~$\overline N^{(1)}:=\overline Z$.\\
          \BlankLine
          
          
      {\renewcommand{\nl}{\let\nl\nl} \tcc{Note that~$((\lambda_\ell,\overline \imath_\ell, \varepsilon_\ell))_{1\leq \ell\leq k-1}$ and~$\overline N^{(k-1)}$ have been defined at the previous step.}}
      Set~$k\leftarrow k+1$ and compute the least-squares fit 
      \[
      \overline \theta_j:=\big(\overline R_{j,\overline \imath_1} \cdots \overline R_{j,\overline \imath_{k-1}}  \big) M^{-1}_{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}} (\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_{k-1})\,,\quad j=1,\ldots,p\,,
      \]
      where~$ M_{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}}$ is the sub-matrix of~$\overline R$ keeping the columns and the rows indexed by~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\}$.
      
      
      
      For~$0<\lambda\leq\lambda_{k-1}$ compute the ‘‘residuals''~$\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda)=(\overline N^{(k)}_1(\lambda),\ldots,\overline N^{(k)}_p(\lambda))$ given by
      \[
      \overline N_j^{(k)}(\lambda):=\overline N_j^{(k-1)}-(\lambda_{k-1}-\lambda)\overline\theta_j\,,\quad j=1,\ldots,p\,,
      \]
and pick
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{k}	&:=\max\big\{\beta>0\, ;\  \exists\, j\notin \{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\},\ 
			\mathrm{s.t.}\ |\overline N_j^{(k)}(\beta)|=\beta\big\}\ \mathrm{and}\ 
\overline \imath_k		:=arg\, max_{j\notin \{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\}} |\overline N_j^{(k)}(\lambda_k)|\,,\\
\varepsilon_k	&:=\overline N_{\overline \imath_k}^{(k)}(\lambda_k)/\lambda_k\in\pm1\ \mathrm{and}\ 
\overline N^{(k)}	:=\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda_k)\,.
\end{align*}
     
 Then, iterate from {\bf 2}.
          \BlankLine
\caption{LARS algorithm (standard formulation)}

Set~$k\leftarrow k+1$ and compute the least-squares fit 
      \[
      \overline \theta_j:=\big(\overline R_{j,\overline \imath_1} \cdots \overline R_{j,\overline \imath_{k-1}}  \big) M^{-1}_{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}} (\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_{k-1})\,,\quad j=1,\ldots,p\,,
      \]
      where~$ M_{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}}$ is the sub-matrix of~$\overline R$ keeping the columns and the rows indexed by~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\}$.

nodes.name: Next knot and iterate
nodes.statement_short: Move residuals linearly in $\lambda$; the next knot is the largest $\lambda$ where an inactive variable ties; iterate.
nodes.statement:
For~$0<\lambda\leq\lambda_{k-1}$ compute the ‘‘residuals''~$\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda)=(\overline N^{(k)}_1(\lambda),\ldots,\overline N^{(k)}_p(\lambda))$ given by
      \[
      \overline N_j^{(k)}(\lambda):=\overline N_j^{(k-1)}-(\lambda_{k-1}-\lambda)\overline\theta_j\,,\quad j=1,\ldots,p\,,
      \]
and pick
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{k}	&:=\max\big\{\beta>0\, ;\  \exists\, j\notin \{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\},\ 
			\mathrm{s.t.}\ |\overline N_j^{(k)}(\beta)|=\beta\big\}\ \mathrm{and}\ 
\overline \imath_k		:=arg\, max_{j\notin \{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}\}} |\overline N_j^{(k)}(\lambda_k)|\,,\\
\varepsilon_k	&:=\overline N_{\overline \imath_k}^{(k)}(\lambda_k)/\lambda_k\in\pm1\ \mathrm{and}\ 
\overline N^{(k)}	:=\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda_k)\,.
\end{align*}
     
 Then, iterate from {\bf 2}.

nodes.name: LARS algorithm (projected formulation)
input: Correlations vector~$\overline Z$ and variance-covariance matrix~$\overline R$.
output: Sequence~$((\lambda_k,\overline \imath_k, \varepsilon_k))_{k\geq1}$ where~$\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\geq\ldots>0$ are the knots, and~$\overline \imath_1,\overline \imath_2,\ldots$ are the variables that enter the model with signs~$\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\ldots$~$(\varepsilon_k=\pm1)$.
nodes.statement_short: LARS knots as maxima of projected, rescaled correlations $(Z_j-\Pi(Z_j))/(1-\theta_j)$ over the signed variables.
nodes.section: 5.1 The equivalent formulations of the~LARS algorithm
nodes.label: alg:LAR2

nodes.name: Initialize
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrize correlations; first knot is $\max Z$.
nodes.statement: Define~$Z=(\overline Z,-\overline Z)$ and~$R$ as in~\eqref{eq:white}, and set~$k=1$,~$\displaystyle \lambda_1:=\max Z~$,~$\displaystyle \widehat \imath_1:=\arg\max Z$,~$\overline \imath_1=\widehat \imath_1 \mod p$ and~$\varepsilon_1=1-2(\,\widehat \imath_1-\overline \imath_1)/p\in\pm1$.
nodes.section: 5.1 The equivalent formulations of the~LARS algorithm

nodes.name: Next knot and iterate
nodes.statement_short: Next knot and signed variable maximize $(Z_j-\Pi(Z_j))/(1-\theta_j)$ over $\theta_j<1$; iterate.
nodes.section: 5.1 The equivalent formulations of the~LARS algorithm
nodes.label: alg:LAR2

nodes.name: Knots of the LARS path
nodes.genus: change points of the LARS path
nodes.statement: The LARS outputs a piecewise affine solutions path, and the {\it knots}~$\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2\geq \dots >0$ are the change points of the LARS path that are built by tracking the~$\ell_{\infty}$ of the residual.
nodes.section: 5.2 A new formulation of Least Angle Regression algorithm

nodes.name: LARS knots versus LASSO knots
nodes.origin_citation: Hastie, Tibshirani & Wainwright 2015; Efron et al. 2004
nodes.statement: This sequence of knots is closely related to the sequence of knots of LASSO~\citep{tibshirani1996regression}, as they differ by only one rule: ‘‘{\it Only in the LASSO case, if a nonzero coefficient crosses zero before the next variable enters, drop it from the active set and recompute the current joint least-squares direction}'', as mentioned in~\cite[Page 120]{hastie2015statistical} or~\cite[Theorem 1]{efron2004least} for instance.

nodes.name: Equivalence of the three LARS formulations

conclusions: then Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} (LARS standard formulation), Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR2} (LARS projected formulation) and  Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR3} (LARS recursive formulation) output the same sequence~$((\lambda_k,\overline \imath_k, \varepsilon_k))_{k=1}^r$ from the input given by~$\overline Z=X^\top Y$ and~$\overline R=X^\top X$

Given a vector~$Y\in\mathbb R^n$ and matrix~$X\in\mathds R^{n\times p}$ of rank~$r$ then Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} (LARS standard formulation), Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR2} (LARS projected formulation) and  Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR3} (LARS recursive formulation) output the same sequence~$((\lambda_k,\overline \imath_k, \varepsilon_k))_{k=1}^r$ from the input given by~$\overline Z=X^\top Y$ and~$\overline R=X^\top X$, where~$\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\geq\lambda_2\ldots\geq0$ are the knots, and~$\overline \imath_1,\overline \imath_2,\ldots,\overline \imath_r$ are the variables that enter the model with signs~$\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\ldots,\varepsilon_r$~$(\varepsilon_k=\pm1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalence of LARS formulations: first knot
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the first two LARS knots with the symmetrized correlations: $\lambda_2$ is the max of $(Z_j-\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1}(Z_j))/(1-\theta_j)$.
nodes.statement:
The first step of the~LARS algorithm (Step {\bf 1} in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}) seeks the most correlated predictor with the observation. In our formulation, introduce the first residual~$N^{(1)}:=Z$ and observe that~$N^{(1)}:=(\overline N^{(1)},-\overline N^{(1)})$. We define the first knot~$\lambda_1>0$ as 
\[
\lambda_1=\displaystyle\max Z\quad \mathrm{and}\quad\widehat \imath _1 = arg\, max Z\,.
\]  
\noindent
One may see that this definition is consistent with~$\lambda_1$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} and note that~$\widehat \imath_1$ and~$(\overline \imath_1,\varepsilon_1)$ are related as in~\eqref{eq:signed_indices}.


The~LARS  algorithm is a forward algorithm that selects a new variable and maintains a residual at each step.  We also define
\begin{equation} N^{(2)}(\lambda)=N^{(1)} - (\lambda_1-\lambda) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)\,,\quad 0<\lambda\leq\lambda_1\,,
\end{equation}
and one can check that~$N^{(2)}(\lambda)=(\overline N^{(2)}(\lambda),-\overline N^{(2)}(\lambda))$ where~$\overline N(\lambda)$ is defined in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}. It is clear that the coordinate~$\widehat \imath_1$ of~$  N^{(2)}(\lambda)$  is equal to~$\lambda$. On the other hand~$  N^{(1)}=Z$ attains  its maximum  at the single point~$\widehat \imath_1$. By continuity  this last property is kept   for~$\lambda$ in a left neighborhood of~$\lambda_1$. We search for the first value of~$\lambda$ such that this property is not met, {\it i.e.} the~largest value of~$\lambda$ such that 
$$
 \exists j \neq \widehat \imath_1 \mbox{ such that }     N^{(2)}(\lambda)  = \lambda\,,
~$$
 as in Step~${\bf 3}$ of Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}. We call this value~$\lambda_2$ and one may check that this definition is consistent with~$\lambda_2$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}. 
 
 Now, we can be more explicit about the expression of~$\lambda_2$. Indeed, we make the following discussion on the values of~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)~$.
 \begin{itemize}
 \item If~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)  \geq 1$ ,  since~$N^{(1)}_j  <N^{(1)}_{\widehat \imath_1}$ for~$j\neq \widehat \imath_1$ there is no hope to achieve the equality  between~$N^{(2)}_j(\lambda)~$ and~$N^{(2)}_{\widehat \imath_1}(\lambda)=\lambda$ for~$0<\lambda\leq\lambda_1$ in view of~\eqref{eq:recu_res}.
 \item   Thus we limit our attention  to the~$j$'s such that~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1) < 1$. We have equality~$N_j^{(2)}(\lambda)  = \lambda$  when
\[
 \lambda =   \frac{N^{(1)}_j -\lambda_1 \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}.
\]
 \end{itemize}
So we can also define the second  knot~$\lambda_2$ of the~LARS  as 
\[
 \lambda_2 
 
  =\max_{j: \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1) 
  < 1} 
  \bigg\{\frac{Z_j -\Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}(Z_j)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}\bigg\}\,.
\]
where~$\Pi_{i_1}(Z_j):=Z_{i_1}\theta_j(i_1)$. Remark that~$\Pi_{i_1}(Z_j)=\mathds{E}(Z_j\ |\ Z_{i_1})$ is the regression of~$Z_j$ on~$Z_{i_1}$ when $\mathds{E} Z=0$.

\[
 \lambda =   \frac{N^{(1)}_j -\lambda_1 \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}.
\]

nodes.statement_short: Discuss according to the value of $\theta_j(\widehat\imath_1)$.
nodes.statement: Now, we can be more explicit about the expression of~$\lambda_2$. Indeed, we make the following discussion on the values of~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)~$.

nodes.name: Case theta >= 1
nodes.statement_short: If $\theta_j\ge1$ coordinate $j$ never ties.
nodes.statement: If~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)  \geq 1$ ,  since~$N^{(1)}_j  <N^{(1)}_{\widehat \imath_1}$ for~$j\neq \widehat \imath_1$ there is no hope to achieve the equality  between~$N^{(2)}_j(\lambda)~$ and~$N^{(2)}_{\widehat \imath_1}(\lambda)=\lambda$ for~$0<\lambda\leq\lambda_1$ in view of~\eqref{eq:recu_res}.

nodes.statement_short: If $\theta_j<1$ solve the tie equation for $\lambda$.
nodes.statement:
Thus we limit our attention  to the~$j$'s such that~$\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1) < 1$. We have equality~$N_j^{(2)}(\lambda)  = \lambda$  when
\[
 \lambda =   \frac{N^{(1)}_j -\lambda_1 \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}.
\]

nodes.statement:
So we can also define the second  knot~$\lambda_2$ of the~LARS  as 
\[
 \lambda_2 
 
  =\max_{j: \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1) 
  < 1} 
  \bigg\{\frac{Z_j -\Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}(Z_j)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1)}\bigg\}\,.

where~$\Pi_{i_1}(Z_j):=Z_{i_1}\theta_j(i_1)$. Remark that~$\Pi_{i_1}(Z_j)=\mathds{E}(Z_j\ |\ Z_{i_1})$ is the regression of~$Z_j$ on~$Z_{i_1}$ when $\mathds{E} Z=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalence of LARS formulations: next knots
nodes.statement_short: By recursion on $k$, the residuals reduce (Lemma) to $Z-\Pi(Z)$, giving the projected formulation of the knots.
nodes.statement:
The loop~$({\bf 2}\rightleftarrows{\bf 3})$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} builds iteratively the knots~$\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ldots$ of the~LARS algorithm and some ‘‘residuals''~$\overline N^{(1)},\overline N^{(2)},\ldots$ defined in Step {\bf 3}. We will present here an equivalent formulation of these knots. 

Assume that~$k\geq2$ and we have build~$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{k-1}$ and selected the ‘‘signed'' variables~$\widehat \imath_1, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$. Introduce~$ N^{(k-1)}:=(\overline N^{(k-1)},-\overline N^{(k-1)})$ and define
 \[
 N^{(k)}(\lambda)=N^{(k-1)}-(\lambda_{k-1}-\lambda) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})\,,\quad 0<\lambda\leq\lambda_{k-1}\,.
  \]
 Check that~$ \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})=(\overline \theta_j,-\overline \theta_j)$ where we recall that we define 
 \[
      \overline \theta_j:=\big(\overline R_{j,\overline \imath_1} \cdots \overline R_{j,\overline \imath_{k-1}}  \big) M^{-1}_{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_{k-1}} (\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_{k-1})\,,\quad j=1,\ldots,p\,,
      \]
      at Step~${\bf 2}$ and it holds that~$\widehat \imath_\ell$ and~$(\overline \imath_\ell,\varepsilon_\ell)$ are related as in~\eqref{eq:signed_indices}. From this equality, we deduce that it holds~$N^{(k)}(\lambda)=(\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda),-\overline N^{(k)}(\lambda))$. One may also check that the coordinates~$\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$ of~$  N^{(k)}(\lambda)$  are equal to~$\lambda$.

Again  if we want to solve~$  N_j^{(k)}(\lambda) = \lambda 
$ for some~$j$, we have to limit our attention  to~$j$'s such that~$  \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}) <1$. Solving this latter equality yields to
 \[
 \lambda_k=  \max_{j : \theta_j( \widehat \imath_1, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) <1} 
 \bigg\{\frac{N^{(k-1)}_j -\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1})}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1})}
 \bigg\}
 \,.
 \]
 This expression is consistent with~$\lambda_k$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}. 
 
 \newpage
 
 Now, we can give an other expression of~$\lambda_k$ that will be useful in the proofs of our main theorems. Note that the residuals satisfy the relation
 \begin{equation} N^{(k)}=N^{(k-1)}-(\lambda_{k-1}-\lambda_k) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})\,,
 \end{equation}
 and that~$N^{(k-1)}_j = \lambda_{k-1}$ for~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$. The following lemma permits  a drastic simplification of the expression of the knots. Its proof is given in Appendix~\ref{proof:ydc1}.
 
    \begin{lemma} It holds 
  \[
 {N^{(k-1)} -\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1})}=Z - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)
  \]
where we denote~$\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z) = (\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_1),\ldots,\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{2p}))$ and note that, for all~$j\in[2p]$, one has $
\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j) =  \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}  
(Z_{i_1}, \ldots, Z_{i_{k-1}})$. 
\end{lemma}

\noindent 
Using Lemma~\ref{l:jm} we deduce that~$\lambda_k$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR} is consistent with
 \begin{equation} \lambda_k=  \max_{j : \theta_j( \widehat \imath_1, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) <1} 
\bigg\{ \frac{Z_j - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z_j)}{ 1-\theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1})}\bigg\}\,.
 \end{equation}
 where~$
\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}} (Z_j) =  \big(R_{j,\widehat\imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat\imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-1}}  
(Z_{\widehat\imath_1}, \ldots, Z_{\widehat\imath_{k-1}})$. When~$\mathds{E} Z=0$, one may remark that $\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)$ is the regression of~$Z_j~$ on the vector~$ (Z_{i_1}, \cdots , Z_{i_{k-1}})$ whose variance-covariance matrix is~$M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}$. This analysis leads to an equivalent formulation of the~LARS algorithm (Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR}). We present this formulation in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR2}.

\begin{align*}

&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1\big\}\,,

nodes.name: Proof of the equivalence of LARS formulations: recursive form
nodes.statement_short: Iterated projections give rank-one updates of $R(k)$, $Z(k)$ and $T(k)$, i.e. the recursive formulation.
nodes.statement:
Now, we present Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR3}. Define~$R(0):=R$,~$Z(0)=Z$ and~$T(0)=0$. For~$k\geq1$ and~$i_1, \ldots, i_{k}\in[2p]$, introduce
\begin{align*}
R(k)&:=\Big({R_{j,\ell} - \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} \big(R_{\ell, i_1} ,\cdots ,R_{ \ell, i_{k}} \big)}\Big)_{j,\ell}\\
Z(k)&:=Z-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z)\\
T(k)&:=(\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k}))_j\,,
\end{align*}
and note that~$R(k)$ is the variance-covariance matrix of the Gaussian vector~$Z(k)$. The key property is following. Let~$v_1,  \ldots, v_k,$ be~$k$ linearly independent vectors of an Euclidean space and let~$u$ be any vector of the space. Set
\[
v:=  P_{(v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1})} ^\perp v_k,
\] 
the  projection of~$v_k$ orthogonally to~$v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1}$.Then 
\[ 
 P_{(v_1, \ldots, v_k)}^\perp u = P_{v}^\perp P_{(v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1})} u\,.
\]
Using this result we deduce that
\begin{align}
Z(k)
&=\Pi^\perp_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z)\notag\\
&=\Pi^\perp_{ i_{k}}(\Pi^\perp_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z))\notag\\
&=\Pi^\perp_{ i_{k}}(Z(k-1))\notag\\
&=Z(k-1)-\Pi_{ i_{k}}(Z(k-1))\notag\\
&=Z(k-1)-{\bf x}(k) Z(k-1) \,,
\end{align}
where~${\bf x}(k)=R_{i_k}(k-1)/R_{i_k,i_k}(k-1)$. It yields that 
\begin{equation} R(k)=R(k-1)-{\bf x}(k) R_{i_k}(k-1)^\top\,.
\end{equation}
Using~\eqref{eq:sign_tau} (or~\eqref{eq:rec101}), remark that 
\begin{align}
T(k)
&=T(k-1)-{\bf x}(k) (1-T_{i_k}(k-1)) \,.
\end{align}
These relations give a recursive formulation of the~LARS as presented in Algorithm~\ref{alg:LAR3}.

nodes.name: Proof of the characterization of the selection event
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ via the frozen-residual recursion for the event; Gaussian regression and norm-direction independence for the second point.
nodes.statement:
{\bf First and third points: } The first point works by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the second point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}. We will use Proposition~\ref{prop:moulinette} to prove the first point. We have
\begin{align}
&\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j-Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{i_k}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}-Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})} \\
&\Leftrightarrow
\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}= Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\,.
\end{align}
using~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj} and that~$1-{\tau_{j,i_k}}/{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}>0$ (which is a consequence of~\eqref{eq:sign_tau} and~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath})  in~\eqref{eq:rec_sign1}. By induction and using~\eqref{eq:rec_sign1}, it holds that
\begin{align*}
\big\{
&\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\big\}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\big\}\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}\,,\ 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\\
&\quad\quad \text{and }\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\  Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\big\}\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1} \text{ and }\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}=Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\big\}\\
&\ \  \vdots\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}_{a}\leq Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\\
&\quad\quad  \text{ and }\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}= Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\leq\ldots\leq \lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}_{a}=Z_{i_a}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}
\big\}\tag{$s_a$} \\
&\ \  \vdots\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k}=i_{k}\big\}\,.
\end{align*}
Now, observe that~$\widehat i_{k+1}$ is the (unique) arg max of~$\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ on the event~$\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k}=i_{k}\big\}$. 


\noindent It yields that 
\begin{align*}
\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k+1}=i_{k+1}\big\}=\big\{
\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}=Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\cdots, i_{k})}
\leq 
Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\cdots, i_{k-1})}\leq\cdots\leq 
Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq
Z_{i_1}\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
as claimed. Stopping at~$a$ as in~\eqref{eq:stopa} gives the second part of the statement. The third point of the proposition is a direct consequence of the first point.

\medskip

\noindent
{\bf Second point: }The proof of the second point can be lead by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the first point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}. Now, observe that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are measurable functions of~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ and one may check that~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ is independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. We deduce that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. One can also check that~$Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ is independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k+1}}$.  Deduce that the variables $Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent and independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$. This gives the first part of the second point of the proposition. 

Now observe that $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$ is a linear function of $P^\perp_{K}Y$. More precisely, consider the vector $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. The key remark is that the direction and the norm of a centered Gaussian vector are independent, namely $\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ is independent of $P_K^\perp(Y)/\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ when $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$. Observe that $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=P_K^\perp(X\beta^0)$ and $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$ is equivalent to $X\beta^0\in H_K$. We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Second point
nodes.statement_short: Prove independence statements.
nodes.statement:
{\bf Second point: }The proof of the second point can be lead by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the first point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}. Now, observe that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are measurable functions of~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ and one may check that~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ is independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. We deduce that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. One can also check that~$Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ is independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k+1}}$.  Deduce that the variables $Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent and independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$. This gives the first part of the second point of the proposition. 

Now observe that $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$ is a linear function of $P^\perp_{K}Y$. More precisely, consider the vector $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. The key remark is that the direction and the norm of a centered Gaussian vector are independent, namely $\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ is independent of $P_K^\perp(Y)/\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ when $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$. Observe that $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=P_K^\perp(X\beta^0)$ and $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$ is equivalent to $X\beta^0\in H_K$. We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement_short: Induction with base case from the first-knot lemma.
nodes.statement: The proof of the second point can be lead by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the first point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}.

nodes.name: Independence of frozen knots
nodes.statement_short: Measurability and Gaussian independence propagate to all frozen knots.
nodes.statement:
Now, observe that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are measurable functions of~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ and one may check that~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ is independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. We deduce that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. One can also check that~$Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ is independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k+1}}$.  Deduce that the variables $Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent and independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$. This gives the first part of the second point of the proposition.

nodes.name: Linear function of residual
nodes.statement_short: Frozen residuals are a linear function of $P_K^\perp Y$.
nodes.statement:
Now observe that $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$ is a linear function of $P^\perp_{K}Y$. More precisely, consider the vector $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
