nodes.name: Norm-direction independence
nodes.statement_short: Norm and direction of a centered Gaussian vector are independent.
nodes.statement: The key remark is that the direction and the norm of a centered Gaussian vector are independent, namely $\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ is independent of $P_K^\perp(Y)/\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ when $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$. Observe that $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=P_K^\perp(X\beta^0)$ and $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$ is equivalent to $X\beta^0\in H_K$. We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of the uniform law of the transformed knots
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the joint density, use centering under the null and admissibility to condition on $\widehat m=a$, then change variables by the CDFs.
nodes.statement:
Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}. From Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1} (more precisely~\eqref{zaz0}) we know that the density of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on 
\[
 \mathcal F:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,
 \]
 is given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \notag
    (const)   \Big(\prod_{k=a+1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)\Big)\, \mathds{1}_{\lambda_a \leq \ell_{a+1}\leq \cdots \leq \ell_K\leq  \lambda_{K+1}}\,.
   \end{equation}
   From Proposition~\ref{prop:H0}, conditional on~$\mathcal F$ and under the null hypothesis described in Proposition \ref{cor:Main1}, we know that~$m_{a+1}=\ldots=m_K=0$. It implies that~$\Phi_k$ is the CDF of~$\lambda_k$ for~$a<k\leq K$. 
 
From the definition of a stopping time given by~\eqref{e:stopping_rule} and on the event~$\mathcal F$, we know that~$\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is a measurable function of~$\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{a-1}$ which are respectively equal to~$Z_{i_1},\ldots,  Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}$ on~$\mathcal F$ by~\eqref{e:frozen} (as proven in Appendix~\ref{app:recursion}  and Eq.~\eqref{e:lambda_max}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} (more precisely~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}), we also know that this function is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. Remark that its is also independent of~$\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional of~$\mathcal F$ for the same reason (it would be useful later, when we will build testing procedures when the variance is unknown). We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event 
 \[
 \mathcal G:=\big\{\widehat m =a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,.
 \]
From~$F_k=\Phi_k(\lambda_k)$ ({\it i.e.,} applying the CDF) we deduce by a change of variables that conditional on the selection event~$ \mathcal G$, the vector~$(F_{a+1},\ldots,F_K)$ is uniformly distributed on 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{D}_{a+1,K}:=&
\big\{
(f_{a+1},\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^{K-a}:\ \\
&\mathcal{P}_{a+1,a}(F_{a})\geq f_{a+1}\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,a+2}(f_{a+2})

\geq \cdots
\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K}(f_K)\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K+1}(F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}$ are described in~\eqref{eq:pij}.

nodes.name: Conditional density
nodes.statement_short: Conditional density of the later knots from the joint law.
nodes.statement:
Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}. From Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1} (more precisely~\eqref{zaz0}) we know that the density of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on 
\[
 \mathcal F:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,
 \]
 is given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \notag
    (const)   \Big(\prod_{k=a+1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)\Big)\, \mathds{1}_{\lambda_a \leq \ell_{a+1}\leq \cdots \leq \ell_K\leq  \lambda_{K+1}}\,.
   \end{equation}

nodes.name: Centering under the null
nodes.statement_short: Under the null the means vanish, so $\Phi_k$ is the CDF of $\lambda_k$.
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{prop:H0}, conditional on~$\mathcal F$ and under the null hypothesis described in Proposition \ref{cor:Main1}, we know that~$m_{a+1}=\ldots=m_K=0$. It implies that~$\Phi_k$ is the CDF of~$\lambda_k$ for~$a<k\leq K$.

nodes.name: Condition on model size
nodes.statement_short: Admissibility and independence allow conditioning on $\widehat m=a$.
nodes.statement:
From the definition of a stopping time given by~\eqref{e:stopping_rule} and on the event~$\mathcal F$, we know that~$\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is a measurable function of~$\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{a-1}$ which are respectively equal to~$Z_{i_1},\ldots,  Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}$ on~$\mathcal F$ by~\eqref{e:frozen} (as proven in Appendix~\ref{app:recursion}  and Eq.~\eqref{e:lambda_max}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} (more precisely~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}), we also know that this function is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. Remark that its is also independent of~$\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional of~$\mathcal F$ for the same reason (it would be useful later, when we will build testing procedures when the variance is unknown). We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event 
 \[
 \mathcal G:=\big\{\widehat m =a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,.
 \]

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement_short: Change of variables gives the uniform law on the domain.
nodes.statement:
From~$F_k=\Phi_k(\lambda_k)$ ({\it i.e.,} applying the CDF) we deduce by a change of variables that conditional on the selection event~$ \mathcal G$, the vector~$(F_{a+1},\ldots,F_K)$ is uniformly distributed on 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{D}_{a+1,K}:=&
\big\{
(f_{a+1},\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^{K-a}:\ \\
&\mathcal{P}_{a+1,a}(F_{a})\geq f_{a+1}\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,a+2}(f_{a+2})

\geq \cdots
\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K}(f_K)\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K+1}(F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}$ are described in~\eqref{eq:pij}.

nodes.name: Proof of the conditional CDF of a knot
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the uniform law, then de-condition since $\mathds F_{abc}$ depends only on $\sigma$, $\lambda_a$, $\lambda_c$ and the middle indices.

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the uniform law to get the conditional CDF.

nodes.name: Dependence of F_abc
nodes.statement_short: $\mathds F_{abc}$ depends on few variables.
nodes.statement: Then note that the function~$\mathds{F}_{abc}$ is defined by~$\sigma,\lambda_a,\lambda_c,\widehat \imath_{a+1}, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{c-1}$ only.

nodes.name: De-condition
nodes.statement_short: De-condition on the other variables.
nodes.statement: We deduce that we can de-condition on~$\widehat m =a, \widehat \imath_{1},\ldots,\widehat \imath_{a}, \widehat \imath_{c},\ldots,\widehat \imath_{K}$, which gives the result.

nodes.name: Proof of independence of the knots and the variance estimator
nodes.statement_short: Frozen knots are independent of $\widehat\sigma$; on the selection event they are the knots, and $\widehat\sigma$ is the norm of a truncated Gaussian vector.
nodes.statement:
Let us fix some values~$i_1, \ldots, i_{K+1}$. Recall  that the frozen values of the knots
\begin{equation}
\notag
 \lambda^f_1 : = Z_{i_1}, \ldots , \lambda^f_{K} :=Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}},\lambda^f_{K+1} :=   Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{i_{K+1}},
  \end{equation}
  are Gaussian, independent, and 
 $
\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} \big(Z_{i_{K+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}\big)
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} \cdots 
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_1}
$, see Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} and~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}. Let us condition by~$\{\widehat\imath_1=i_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K=i_K, \lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1}\}$. Note that, on this event,~$ \lambda_h^f = \lambda_h$ ,~$h \in [K]$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} this event is equivalent  to 
 \begin{equation} \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
\end{equation} 
Because of the independence above, we get the conditional independence stated in the first and second point of the proposition. 

\noindent
For the last point, consider $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. Now, let $U\in\mathds R^{n\times (n-K)}$ be any matrix such that $UU^\top=P_K^\perp$ and define $W:=U^\top Y/\sigma$, then 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\sigma\times\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\,.
\]
Because of the independence above and \eqref{e:se_prop}, the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma$ is independent of the other variables and such that 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}\quad\mathrm{with\ }W\mathrm{\ s.t.\ }\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\ell_{K+1}/\sigma\,.
\]
This implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.name: Recall independence
nodes.statement_short: Recall independence of the frozen knots and $\widehat\sigma$.

nodes.name: Condition on selection
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the selection event characterized by the proposition.
nodes.statement:
Let us condition by~$\{\widehat\imath_1=i_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K=i_K, \lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1}\}$. Note that, on this event,~$ \lambda_h^f = \lambda_h$ ,~$h \in [K]$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} this event is equivalent  to 
 \begin{equation} \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
\end{equation} 
Because of the independence above, we get the conditional independence stated in the first and second point of the proposition.

nodes.name: Equation (7.2)
nodes.statement: \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
nodes.label: e:se_prop

nodes.name: Represent via W
nodes.statement_short: Express $\widehat\sigma$ and the frozen residuals via $W=U^\top Y/\sigma$.
nodes.statement:
For the last point, consider $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,

\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\sigma\times\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\,.
\]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Truncation of $W$ gives the law of $\widehat\sigma$.
nodes.statement:
Because of the independence above and \eqref{e:se_prop}, the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma$ is independent of the other variables and such that 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}\quad\mathrm{with\ }W\mathrm{\ s.t.\ }\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\ell_{K+1}/\sigma\,.
\]
This implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of uniformly most powerful GSt in the orthogonal design
nodes.statement_short: Three monotonicity steps (in $c$, $b$, $a$); each compares rejection regions of equal null mass and uses a measure transport with a coordinate-wise nondecreasing alternative density.
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal I$ the set of admissible indexes 
~$$
 \mathcal I := \{a,b,c: a_0\leq a<b<c \leq K+1 \}\,.
~$$

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig1.png}

\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig2.png}
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig3.png}
\caption{Rejection domains associated to the different comparison sets appearing in steps of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:zazPower}.} \end{figure}

 
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 1: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes such that~$c+1\leq K+1$ belong to~$\mathcal I$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. Our proof is conditional to~$F_a=f_a,F_{c+1} =f_{c+1}~$.  Note that~$(F_{a+1}, \ldots, F_c)~$ has for distribution the uniform distribution  on the simplex
~$$
  \mathcal S := \{ f_a>F_{a+1} > \cdots > F_c >f_{c+1} \}.
~$$ 
  This implies  by direct calculations that 
~$$
  \mathcal{I}_{ab}(s,t) =\frac{ (s-t) ^{b-a-1}}{(b-a-1)!}
~$$
  and that 
\begin{equation} \frac{   \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)   }{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)} = \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta((b-a),(c-b))} \bigg( \frac{ F_b-F_c}{ f_a-F_c} \bigg).
\end{equation}
  where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference.  Using monotony of this  function the~$\mathcal{S}_{abc}$ test has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} (F_b-F_c)  \geq z_1 (f_a-F_c) \Leftrightarrow  F_b \geq z_1 f_a +(1-z_1) F_c,
 \end{equation}
  where~$z_1$ is some threshold, depending on~$\alpha$, that belongs to~$(0,1)$. 
  
  
  Similarly~$\mathcal{S}_{ab(c+1)}$ has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} F_b \geq z_2 (f_a-f_{c+1})  + f_{c+1},
  \end{equation}
  where~$z_2$ is some other threshold belonging to~$(0,1)$. We use the following lemmas.  
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$c \leq K$.  The density~$h_\mu$ of~$f_1, \ldots, f_c$, conditional on~$F_{c+1}$ with respect of the Lebesgue measure  under the alternative is  coordinate-wise  non-decreasing and given by~\eqref{zazcosh}.
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}
Observe that it suffises to prove the result when~$\sigma=1$. Note that 
~$$
 \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1, \dots, i_c } =   \max_{j\in[p]\,,\   j\neq \overline \imath_1,\ldots,   j \neq  \overline \imath_c}  |Z_j|.
~$$
  Thus its density~$ p_{\mu^0,i_1,\ldots,i_c}$ does not depend  on~$\mu^0_{ \overline i_1},\ldots,\mu^0_{ \overline i_c}$. As a consequence the following variables have the same distribution ;
$ \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1 +\epsilon_1 p, \dots, i_c +\epsilon_c p}~$ , where~$\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_c$ take the value 0 or 1 and  indices are taken modulo~$p$. 



Because of the independence of the different variables, the joint density, under the alternative hypothesis, of $\lambda_1, \ldots,  \lambda_{c+1}$ taken at~$ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_{c+1},$  on the domain~$ \{\lambda_1>\cdots > \lambda_{c+1}\}$ takes the value
~$$
 (Const)   \sum'   \big(\varphi(\ell_1 -\mu^0_{j_1} ) +\varphi(\ell_1 +\mu^0_{j_1} ) \big),\ldots ,
   \big(\varphi(\ell_c -\mu^0_{j_c} ) +\varphi(\ell_c +\mu^0_{j_c} ) \big)
  p_{\mu^0,j_1,\ldots,j_K}(\ell_{k+1}).
~$$
Here the sum~$ \displaystyle \sum'$ is taken over all different~$j_1, \ldots, j_c$ belonging  to~$\llbracket 1, p\rrbracket$.
 
 Then the density, conditional on~$F_{c+1} = f_{c+1}$,   of
~$ F_1 ,\ldots,F_{c}~$  at~$f_1,\ldots,f_c$  takes the value
~
\begin{equation} \mathrm{(const)}  \sum'  \cosh( \mu_{j_1} f_1)\ldots \cosh( \mu_{j_c} f_c) \mathds{1}_{f_1>\cdots> f_{c}> F_{c+1}},
\end{equation}
 implying  that this density is coordinate-wise  non-decreasing. 
 \end{proof}
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$\nu_0$  the image  on the plane~$(F_b,F_c)$  on the uniform probability  on~$\mathcal S$: it is the distribution  under the null of~$(F_b,F_c)$. The two rejection regions :~$\mathcal R_1$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r1} and~$\mathcal R_2$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r2} 
have  of course the same probability~$\alpha$ under~$\nu_0$. Let~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ the density w.r.t.~$\nu_0$ of the distribution of~$(F_b,F_c)$ under the alternative. Then~$\eta_{\mu^0}$     is non decreasing coordinate-wise. 
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}  
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]
  The density of~$\nu_{\mu^0}$  w.r.t. Lebesgue measure  is 
  \begin{equation} \int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
 \end{equation}
  Thus~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ which is the quotient  of these two quantities is just  a mean value  of~$h_{\mu^0}$ on the domain  of integration~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}$  in~\eqref{ZAZA:e:vm}.
  
  Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.
\end{proof}

\medskip
   
    \noindent
     {\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.  \bigskip

  
  
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 2: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$. 
 
 
 
 \noindent
  The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form 
~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.  \bigskip



  
  
  
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 3: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a+1<b$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$. 
  Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_{c} =f_{c}~$ and is located in the plane~$F_{a+1}, F_b$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_1 f_a + (1-z_1)f_c~$ for some threshold~$z_1$belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline

These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and  the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is greater of equal  that that of~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$.  \bigskip

\noindent
Considering the three cases above,  we get the desired result.

nodes.name: Admissible indexes
nodes.statement_short: Set of admissible index triples.
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal I$ the set of admissible indexes 
~$$
 \mathcal I := \{a,b,c: a_0\leq a<b<c \leq K+1 \}\,.
~$$

nodes.name: Step 1
nodes.statement_short: Increasing $c$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 1: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes such that~$c+1\leq K+1$ belong to~$\mathcal I$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. Our proof is conditional to~$F_a=f_a,F_{c+1} =f_{c+1}~$.  Note that~$(F_{a+1}, \ldots, F_c)~$ has for distribution the uniform distribution  on the simplex
~$$
  \mathcal S := \{ f_a>F_{a+1} > \cdots > F_c >f_{c+1} \}.
~$$ 
  This implies  by direct calculations that 
~$$
  \mathcal{I}_{ab}(s,t) =\frac{ (s-t) ^{b-a-1}}{(b-a-1)!}
~$$
  and that 
\begin{equation} \frac{   \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)   }{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)} = \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta((b-a),(c-b))} \bigg( \frac{ F_b-F_c}{ f_a-F_c} \bigg).
\end{equation}
  where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference.  Using monotony of this  function the~$\mathcal{S}_{abc}$ test has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} (F_b-F_c)  \geq z_1 (f_a-F_c) \Leftrightarrow  F_b \geq z_1 f_a +(1-z_1) F_c,
 \end{equation}
  where~$z_1$ is some threshold, depending on~$\alpha$, that belongs to~$(0,1)$. 
  
  
  Similarly~$\mathcal{S}_{ab(c+1)}$ has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} F_b \geq z_2 (f_a-f_{c+1})  + f_{c+1},
  \end{equation}
  where~$z_2$ is some other threshold belonging to~$(0,1)$. We use the following lemmas.  
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$c \leq K$.  The density~$h_\mu$ of~$f_1, \ldots, f_c$, conditional on~$F_{c+1}$ with respect of the Lebesgue measure  under the alternative is  coordinate-wise  non-decreasing and given by~\eqref{zazcosh}.
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}
Observe that it suffises to prove the result when~$\sigma=1$. Note that 
~$$
 \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1, \dots, i_c } =   \max_{j\in[p]\,,\   j\neq \overline \imath_1,\ldots,   j \neq  \overline \imath_c}  |Z_j|.
~$$
  Thus its density~$ p_{\mu^0,i_1,\ldots,i_c}$ does not depend  on~$\mu^0_{ \overline i_1},\ldots,\mu^0_{ \overline i_c}$. As a consequence the following variables have the same distribution ;
$ \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1 +\epsilon_1 p, \dots, i_c +\epsilon_c p}~$ , where~$\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_c$ take the value 0 or 1 and  indices are taken modulo~$p$. 



Because of the independence of the different variables, the joint density, under the alternative hypothesis, of $\lambda_1, \ldots,  \lambda_{c+1}$ taken at~$ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_{c+1},$  on the domain~$ \{\lambda_1>\cdots > \lambda_{c+1}\}$ takes the value
~$$
 (Const)   \sum'   \big(\varphi(\ell_1 -\mu^0_{j_1} ) +\varphi(\ell_1 +\mu^0_{j_1} ) \big),\ldots ,
   \big(\varphi(\ell_c -\mu^0_{j_c} ) +\varphi(\ell_c +\mu^0_{j_c} ) \big)
  p_{\mu^0,j_1,\ldots,j_K}(\ell_{k+1}).
~$$
Here the sum~$ \displaystyle \sum'$ is taken over all different~$j_1, \ldots, j_c$ belonging  to~$\llbracket 1, p\rrbracket$.
 
 Then the density, conditional on~$F_{c+1} = f_{c+1}$,   of
~$ F_1 ,\ldots,F_{c}~$  at~$f_1,\ldots,f_c$  takes the value
~
\begin{equation} \mathrm{(const)}  \sum'  \cosh( \mu_{j_1} f_1)\ldots \cosh( \mu_{j_c} f_c) \mathds{1}_{f_1>\cdots> f_{c}> F_{c+1}},
\end{equation}
 implying  that this density is coordinate-wise  non-decreasing. 
 \end{proof}
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$\nu_0$  the image  on the plane~$(F_b,F_c)$  on the uniform probability  on~$\mathcal S$: it is the distribution  under the null of~$(F_b,F_c)$. The two rejection regions :~$\mathcal R_1$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r1} and~$\mathcal R_2$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r2} 
have  of course the same probability~$\alpha$ under~$\nu_0$. Let~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ the density w.r.t.~$\nu_0$ of the distribution of~$(F_b,F_c)$ under the alternative. Then~$\eta_{\mu^0}$     is non decreasing coordinate-wise. 
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}  
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]
  The density of~$\nu_{\mu^0}$  w.r.t. Lebesgue measure  is 
  \begin{equation} \int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
 \end{equation}
  Thus~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ which is the quotient  of these two quantities is just  a mean value  of~$h_{\mu^0}$ on the domain  of integration~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}$  in~\eqref{ZAZA:e:vm}.
  
  Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.
\end{proof}

\medskip
   
    \noindent
     {\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Proof of monotone likelihood ratio
nodes.statement_short: The likelihood ratio is a mean of the monotone density $h_{\mu^0}$ over a domain whose bounds increase with $(f_b,f_c)$.
nodes.statement:
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]
  The density of~$\nu_{\mu^0}$  w.r.t. Lebesgue measure  is 
  \begin{equation} \int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
 \end{equation}
  Thus~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ which is the quotient  of these two quantities is just  a mean value  of~$h_{\mu^0}$ on the domain  of integration~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}$  in~\eqref{ZAZA:e:vm}.
  
  Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.

nodes.name: Null density
nodes.statement_short: Null density of $(F_b,F_c)$.
nodes.statement:
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]

nodes.name: Ratio as mean
nodes.statement_short: Likelihood ratio is a mean of $h_{\mu^0}$.

nodes.name: Equation (7.7)
nodes.statement:
\int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
nodes.label: ZAZA:e:vm

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement_short: Monotone bounds and monotone density give monotone ratio.
nodes.statement: Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.

nodes.name: Finish Step 1
nodes.statement_short: Measure-preserving transport from $A$ to $B$ increases alternative probability.
nodes.statement:
{\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Regions A and B
nodes.statement_short: Regions $A$ and $B$ have equal null measure.
nodes.statement:
For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure.

nodes.name: Separating point
nodes.statement_short: A point $K$ separates $A$ (below-left) from $B$ (above-right).

nodes.name: Points of A
nodes.statement_short: Points of $A$ lie below-left of $K$.
nodes.statement: For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,

nodes.name: Points of B
nodes.statement_short: Points of $B$ lie above-right of $K$.
nodes.statement: For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,

nodes.name: Transport
nodes.statement_short: A measure-preserving map $A\to B$ increases the alternative probability.
nodes.statement:
By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing $b$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 2: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. 
 Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_b =f_b~$ and is located  
 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$. 
 
 
 
 \noindent
  The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form 
~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Conditioning
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $F_a$, $F_b$.
nodes.statement:
We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. 
 Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_b =f_b~$ and is located  
 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$.

nodes.name: Rejection regions
nodes.statement_short: Linear rejection regions.
nodes.statement:
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form 
~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

nodes.name: Conclude Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Transport argument as in Step 1.
nodes.statement: Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Step 3
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing $a$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 3: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a+1<b$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$. 
  Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_{c} =f_{c}~$ and is located in the plane~$F_{a+1}, F_b$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_1 f_a + (1-z_1)f_c~$ for some threshold~$z_1$belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
 The rejection region~$R_{a+1,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_2 F_{a+1} + (1-z_2)f_c ~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and  the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is greater of equal  that that of~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$.

nodes.name: Conditioning
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $F_a$, $F_c$.
nodes.statement:
We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a+1<b$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$. 
  Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_{c} =f_{c}~$ and is located in the plane~$F_{a+1}, F_b$.

nodes.name: Rejection regions
nodes.statement_short: Linear rejection regions.
nodes.statement:
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_1 f_a + (1-z_1)f_c~$ for some threshold~$z_1$belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
 The rejection region~$R_{a+1,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_2 F_{a+1} + (1-z_2)f_c ~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

nodes.name: Conclude Step 3
nodes.statement_short: Transport argument as in Step 1.
nodes.statement: Transport of measure  and  the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is greater of equal  that that of~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Combine the three monotonicity steps.
nodes.statement: Considering the three cases above,  we get the desired result.

nodes.name: Proof of the residual simplification lemma
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ using the residual recursion and the three-perpendicular identity for $\theta$ and $\Pi$.
nodes.statement:
The proof works by induction. Let us check the relation for~$k=2$, namely
\[
 N^{(1)} -\lambda_{1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z-Z_{\widehat \imath_1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}  (Z)\,.
\]
Now, let~$k\geq 3$. First, the three perpendicular theorem  implies  that  for every~$j,  i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}~$,
\begin{align*}
	\theta_j(i_1, \ldots ,  i_{k-2})
   	&= \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}   
		( 
 			\theta_{i_1}(i_1, \ldots ,  i_{k-2}),\ldots,\theta_{i_{k-1}} (i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})  
  		)\,,\\
	\mathrm{and}\ \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_j)
	&= \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}   
		( 
  			\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_{i_1}),\ldots,\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_{i_{k-1}})  
  		)\,.
\end{align*}
By induction, using~\eqref{eq:value_nk}, we get that
\begin{align}
N^{(k-1)}&=N^{(k-2)}-(\lambda_{k-2}-\lambda_{k-1}) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag
\\
&=
(N^{(k-2)}-\lambda_{k-2} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}))+\lambda_{k-1}\theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag\\
&=
Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,. \end{align}
Then, recall that~$N^{(k-1)}_j = \lambda_{k-1}$ for~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$ and remark that
\[
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) 
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})\,.
\]
Using~\eqref{eq:induc} at indices~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$, we deduce that
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,&\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) \\
&
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
& = \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
   (Z_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
 &\quad - \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
	( 
  		\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_1}),\ldots,\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})  
  	)
\\
&\quad + \lambda_{k-1}\big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
( 
 \theta_{\widehat \imath_1}(\,\widehat \imath_1, \ldots , \widehat\imath_{k-2}),\ldots,\theta_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}} (\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2})  
  ) 
\\
& = \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-1}}  (Z_{j})- \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_j)
+\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}) \,,
  \end{align*}
  Namely
  \[
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})
  =
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,.
  \]
Using again~\eqref{eq:induc} we get that
\begin{align*}
 N^{(k-1)}&= Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\\
 &=Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})\,,
\end{align*}
as claimed.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement_short: Base case $k=2$.
nodes.statement:
The proof works by induction. Let us check the relation for~$k=2$, namely
\[
 N^{(1)} -\lambda_{1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z-Z_{\widehat \imath_1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}  (Z)\,.
\]

nodes.name: Three perpendicular theorem
nodes.statement_short: Three perpendicular theorem expresses $\theta$ and $\Pi$ at order $k-2$ via order $k-1$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement_short: Inductive expression of $N^{(k-1)}$.
nodes.statement:
By induction, using~\eqref{eq:value_nk}, we get that
\begin{align}
N^{(k-1)}&=N^{(k-2)}-(\lambda_{k-2}-\lambda_{k-1}) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag
\\
&=
(N^{(k-2)}-\lambda_{k-2} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}))+\lambda_{k-1}\theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag\\
&=
Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,. \end{align}

nodes.name: Equation (7.8)
nodes.statement:
N^{(k-1)}&=N^{(k-2)}-(\lambda_{k-2}-\lambda_{k-1}) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag
\\
&=
(N^{(k-2)}-\lambda_{k-2} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}))+\lambda_{k-1}\theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag\\
&=
Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,.
nodes.label: eq:induc

nodes.name: Projection identity
nodes.statement_short: Compare projections at orders $k-1$ and $k-2$.
nodes.statement:
Then, recall that~$N^{(k-1)}_j = \lambda_{k-1}$ for~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$ and remark that
\[
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) 
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})\,.
\]
Using~\eqref{eq:induc} at indices~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$, we deduce that
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,&\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) \\
&
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
& = \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
   (Z_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
 &\quad - \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
	( 
  		\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_1}),\ldots,\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})  
  	)
\\
&\quad + \lambda_{k-1}\big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
( 
 \theta_{\widehat \imath_1}(\,\widehat \imath_1, \ldots , \widehat\imath_{k-2}),\ldots,\theta_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}} (\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2})  
  ) 
\\
& = \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-1}}  (Z_{j})- \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_j)
+\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}) \,,
  \end{align*}
  Namely
  \[
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})
  =
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,.
  \]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Substitute to conclude.

nodes.name: Proof of the recursion for the frozen residuals
nodes.statement_short: Schur complement and LU block inversion show numerators and denominators of the two expressions coincide.
nodes.statement:
We denote
\begin{align*}
R_{j}&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)\,,\\
R_{i_k}&:=\big(R_{i_k, i_1} ,\ldots ,R_{ i_k, i_{k-1}} \big)\,,\\
M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}\,,\\
\overline M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}M & R_{i_k} \\R_{i_k}^\top & R_{i_k,i_k}\end{array}\right]\,,\\
\overline R&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)\,,\\

x&:=\frac{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}{1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\,,
\end{align*}
and observe that
\begin{align}
x&=\frac
{R_{j,i_k} -R_j^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}
{R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}&=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & -M^{-1}R_{i_k} \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}M^{-1} & 0 \\0 & \big(R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}\big)^{-1}\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & 0 \\-R_{i_k}^{\top}M^{-1} & 1\end{array}\right]\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}\overline R&=
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\,, \end{align}
using Schur complement of block~$M$ of the matrix~$\overline M$ and a LU decomposition. Note also that
\[
\frac{Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j-Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{i_k}\tau_{j,i_k}/\tau_{i_k,i_k}}
{1-\tau_{j,i_k}/\tau_{i_k,i_k}}
=\frac
{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x\,(Z_{i_k}-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k}))}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x(1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}))}\,.
\]
To prove~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj}, it suffices to show that the R.H.S term  above is equal to the following R.H.S term
\[
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j=
\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\,.
\]
We will prove that numerators are equal and that denominators are equal. For denominators, 
\begin{align}
&1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x(1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}))\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x+x\,\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})\notag\\
&=1-(\underbrace{1\cdots 1}_{k\ \mathrm{times}})
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k}) \,,
\end{align}
using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}. Furthermore, it proves~\eqref{eq:sign_tau}. For the numerators, we use that
\begin{align*}
&Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x\,(Z_{i_k}-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k}))\\
&=Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x Z_{i_k}+ x \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k})\\
&=Z_j-(Z_{i_1}\cdots Z_{i_k})
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\\
&=Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)\,.
\end{align*}
using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}.

nodes.name: Schur complement
nodes.statement_short: Notation and block inverse via Schur complement.
nodes.statement:
We denote
\begin{align*}
R_{j}&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)\,,\\
R_{i_k}&:=\big(R_{i_k, i_1} ,\ldots ,R_{ i_k, i_{k-1}} \big)\,,\\
M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}\,,\\
\overline M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}M & R_{i_k} \\R_{i_k}^\top & R_{i_k,i_k}\end{array}\right]\,,\\
\overline R&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)\,,\\

x&:=\frac{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}{1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\,,
\end{align*}
and observe that
\begin{align}
x&=\frac
{R_{j,i_k} -R_j^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}
{R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}&=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & -M^{-1}R_{i_k} \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}M^{-1} & 0 \\0 & \big(R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}\big)^{-1}\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & 0 \\-R_{i_k}^{\top}M^{-1} & 1\end{array}\right]\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}\overline R&=
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\,, \end{align}
using Schur complement of block~$M$ of the matrix~$\overline M$ and a LU decomposition.

nodes.name: Reduction

nodes.statement:
To prove~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj}, it suffices to show that the R.H.S term  above is equal to the following R.H.S term
\[
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j=
\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\,.
\]

using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}. Furthermore, it proves~\eqref{eq:sign_tau}.

nodes.name: Proof of exact FDR control in orthogonal design
nodes.statement_short: Show the p-values are WPRDS: after a change of variables, build a Knothe-Rosenblatt transport map that pushes conditional laws upward coordinate-wise.
nodes.statement:
We rely on the {\bf Weak Positive Regression Dependency (WPRDS) property} to prove the result, one may consult~\cite[Page 173]{giraud2014introduction} for instance. We say that a function~$g:[0,1]^K\to \mathds{R}^+$ is {\it nondecreasing} if for any~$p,q\in[0,1]^K$ such that~$p_k\geq q_k$ for every~$k=1,\ldots, K$, we have~$g(p)\geq g(q)$. We say that a Borel set~$\Gamma\in[0,1]^K$ is {\it nondecreasing} if~$g=\mathds 1_\Gamma$ is nondecreasing. In other words  if~$y \in \gamma$ and if~$z\geq0$, then~$y+z \in \gamma$. We say that the~$p$-values~$(\,\widehat p_1=\widehat\alpha_{0,1,K+1},\ldots,\widehat p_K=\widehat\alpha_{K-1,K,K+1})$ satisfy the WPRDS property if for any nondecreasing set~$\Gamma$ 
 and for all~$k^0\in I_0$, the function 
\[
u\mapsto \mathds{P}_{\mu^0}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
\]
where~$\mu^0=\beta^0$ in our  orthogonal design case, and we recall that
\[
I_0=\big\{k\in[K]\ :\ \mathds H_{0,k}\text{ is true}\big\}\,.
\] 
To prove Theorem \ref{thm:independentTest}, note that it is sufficient~\cite[Chapter~8]{giraud2014introduction} to prove that 
\begin{equation} u\mapsto \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
\end{equation}
where~$\overline{\mathds{E}},\overline{\operatorname{\mathds{P}}}$ will denote that expectations and probabilities are conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$ and under the hypothesis that~$\mu^0=X^\top X\beta^0$. Note that one can integrate in~$\lambda_{K+1}$ to get the statement of Theorem \ref{thm:independentTest}.

\medskip

\noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 1: }We start by giving the joint law of the LARS knots under the alternative in the orthogonal design case. Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} and~\eqref{zazcosh} show that, conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$,~$(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K)$ is distributed on the set~$\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \cdots\geq \lambda_K\geq \lambda_{K+1}$ and it has a coordinate-wise nondecreasing density. 
 
 Now we can assume without loss of generality  that~$\sigma^2 =1$, in addition because of orthogonality 
~$\rho_k^2=1$ implying that~$F_k=\Phi(\lambda_k)$~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}=\Phi_i\circ\Phi_j^{-1}=\mathrm{Id}$.  We deduce that, conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}\}$,~$(F_1,\ldots,F_K)$ is distributed on the set
\[
\big\{
(f_1,\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^K\ :\ 
1\geq f_1\geq f_2\geq \cdots\geq f_K\geq F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\]
it has an {\bf explicit density} given by~\eqref{zazcosh}, and we denote it by~$h_{\mu^0}$. By the change of variables~$G_k:=\frac{ F_k-F_{K+1}}{ F_{k-1}-F_{K+1}}$ one  obtains that the distribution of~$(G_1,\ldots,G_K)$ is supported on~$[0,1]^K$. More precisely, define
\begin{align*}
\psi(f_1,\ldots,f_K)& :=(g_1,\ldots,g_K)   := (\frac{ f_1-F_{K+1}}{1-F_{K+1}},\ldots,\frac{ f_K-F_{K+1}}{f_{K-1}-F_{K+1}}) \\
\psi^{-1}(g_1,\ldots,g_K)&:=\Big((1-F_{K+1})g_1+F_{K+1},\ldots,(1-F_{K+1})g_1g_2\ldots g_K+F_{K+1}\Big),
\end{align*}
whose inverse Jacobian determinant is 
\[
\det\Big[\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial f_1} \cdots\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial f_K}\Big]^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^K(f_{k-1}-F_{K+1})=(1-F_{K+1})^K\prod_{k=1}^{K}g_k^{K-k}\,.
\] 
We deduce that the density  of~$(G_1,\ldots,G_K)|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}\}$  at point~$g$ with respect to Lebesgue measure is 
\begin{align} \mathbf{p}(g):=
\mathrm{(const)}\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}g_k^{K-k}&\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,,
\end{align}
where we have used~\eqref{zazcosh}. From~\eqref{zaza5} and~\eqref{eq:BetaF}, one has 
\begin{equation} \widehat p_k =1-\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)} \bigg( \frac{ F_k-F_{K+1}}{ F_{k-1}-F_{K+1}} \bigg)
=1-\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)}(G_k)
\end{equation}
 where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference. We deduce that for any~$v\in(0,1)$ and for any~$\ell\in[K]$, 
\begin{align*}













\widehat p_k &= v
\Leftrightarrow
(G_1,\ldots,G_K)\in 
{[0,1]^K\cap\{\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)}^{-1}(1-v)= G_k\}
}

\,,
\end{align*}
so that 
\begin{equation} \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]=\overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(G_1,\ldots,G_K)\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-\ell+1)}^{-1}(1-u)\big]\,,
\end{equation}
where~$\overline\Gamma$ can be proved to be a {\bf nonincreasing Borel set} from~\eqref{eq:yoyoFDR}. 


\medskip

\noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 2: }
 Let~$0<x<y<1$ and denote by~$\mu_x$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_x:=\mathrm{law}\big[(G_1,\ldots,G_K)|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1},G_{k^0}\geq x\}\big]\,.
 \] 
 Remark that if there exists a measurable~$T:[0,1]^K\mapsto [0,1]^K$ such that 
 \begin{itemize}
 \item~$T$ is nondecreasing, meaning that for any~$g\in[0,1]^K$,~$T(g)\geq g$;
 \item~$T$ is such that push-forward of~$\mu_x$ by~$T$ gives~$\mu_y$, namely~$T_\#\mu_x=\mu_y$;
 \end{itemize}
then it holds
 \begin{itemize}
 \item~$\mathds 1_{\{T(g)\in\overline\Gamma\}}\leq\mathds 1_{\{g\in\overline\Gamma\}}$;
 \item~$\mathrm{law}\big[T(G)|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1},G_{k^0}\geq x\}\big]=\mathrm{law}\big[G|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1},G_{k^0}\geq y\}\big]$ where~$G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K)$.
 \end{itemize}
In this case, we deduce that 
\[
\overline{\mathds{P}}\big[G\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq x\big]
\geq
\overline{\mathds{P}}\big[T(G)\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq x\big]
=
\overline{\mathds{P}}\big[G\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq y\big]\,.
\]
 If one can prove that such function~$T$ exists for any~$0<x<y<1$, it proves that 
 \[
 x\mapsto \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[G\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq x\big]\text{ is nonincreasing}\,,
 \]
and, in view of~\eqref{yoyo:Fg}, it proves~\eqref{yoyonondecresaing}. Proving that such function~$T$ exists is done in the next step.

\medskip

\noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 3: }
 Let~$0<x<y<1$. Consider the {\bf Knothe-Rosenblatt transport map}~$T$ of~$\mu_x$ toward~$\mu_y$ following the order
 \[
 k^0\to k^0+1\to\cdots\to K\to k^0-1\to k^0-2\to\cdots\to 1\,.
 \]
 It is based on a sequence of conditional quantile transforms defined following the ordering above. Its construction is presented for instance in~\cite[Sec.2.3, P.67]{santambrogio2015optimal} or~\cite[P.20]{villani2008optimal}. The transport~$T$ is defined as follows. Given~$z,z'\in[0,1]^K$ such that~$z'=T(z)$ it holds
 \begin{align*}
 z'_{k^0}&=T^{(k^0)}(z_{k^0});\\
 z'_{k^0+1}&=T^{(k^0+1)}(z_{k^0+1},z'_{k^0});\\
 &\vdots\\
 z'_K&=T^{(K)}(z_K,z'_{K-1},\ldots,z'_{k^0});\\
 z'_{k^0-1}&=T^{(k^0-1)}(z_{k^0-1},z'_K,\ldots,z'_{k^0});\\
 &\vdots\\
 z'_1&=T^{(1)}(z_1,z'_2,\ldots,z'_{k^0-1},z'_K,\ldots,z'_{k^0});
 \end{align*}
where~$T^{(k^0)}, T^{(k^0+1)},\ldots,T^{(K)},T^{(k^0-1)}\ldots,T^{(1)}$ will be build in the sequel, in which we will drop their dependencies in the~$z'_k$'s to ease notations. It remains to prove that 
 \begin{itemize}
 \item~$T$ is nondecreasing, meaning that for any~$g\in[0,1]^K$,~$T(g)\geq g$;
 \item~$T$ is such that push-forward of~$\mu_x$ by~$T$ gives~$\mu_y$, namely~$T_\#\mu_x=\mu_y$;
 \end{itemize}
 to conclude. The last point is a property of the Knothe-Rosenblatt transport map. Proving the first point will be done in the rest of  the proof.
 
 \medskip
 
\noindent
 {$\circ$ \it Step 3.1: } We start by the first transport map~$T^{(k^0)}:[0,1]\mapsto[0,1]$. Denote~$\mu_x^{(k^0)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_x^{(k^0)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k^0}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1},G_{k^0}\geq x\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}$ its cdf. Note that the Knothe-Rosenblatt construction gives~$T^{(k^0)}=(\mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)})^{-1}\circ\mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}$. We would like to prove that~$T^{(k^0)}(t)\geq t$ for all~$z\in(0,1)$. This is equivalent to prove that it holds~$ \mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}\geq \mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)}$. For~$t\leq y$,~$\mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)}(t)=0$ and it implies that~$ \mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}(t)\geq \mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)}(t)$. Let~$t>y$, using the conditional density~$\mathbf{p}$ defined in~\eqref{eq:density}, note that
 
 \begin{align*}
 \mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}(t)\geq \mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)}(t)\quad&\Leftrightarrow\quad 
 \frac  {\int_x^t\mathbf{p}}  {\int_x^1\mathbf{p}}    \geq 
 \frac  {\int_y^t\mathbf{p}}  {\int_y^1\mathbf{p}} \\
 &\Leftrightarrow\quad \int_x^t \int_y^1 \mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}
 
 \geq \int_y^t   \int_x^1\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p},
 \end{align*}
where, for example
\[
\int_x^t \mbox{ means the integral over the  hyper rectangle }  [x,t]
:=\Big\{(g_1,\ldots,g_K)\in[0,1]^K\ :\!\ x\leq g_{k^0}\leq t\Big\}.
\]
A simple calculation (see also Figure~\ref{fig:yoyo}) gives that
\[
\int_x^t \int_y^1 \mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p} = \int_y^t   \int_x^1\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p} +
\int_{[x,y] \times [t,1]}
\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}\,,
\]
and it proves that~$ \mathds{F}_x^{(k^0)}\geq \mathds{F}_y^{(k^0)}$.

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width=0.4\textwidth]{y1}
\caption{Note that, by symmetry  the two boxed regions  have same~$ \mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}$ measure. The blue region is~$[x,t]\times [y,1]~$, its measure is the measure of the red region (namely~$cD_y(t)\times \mathcal{D}_x(1)$) more the bluest upper left corner (namely~$ [x,y]\times[t,1]$). } \end{figure}
 
 \medskip
 
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \it Step 3.2: } We continue with the second transport map in Knothe-Rosenblatt construction. Let~$z_{k^0}\in(x,1)$ and denote~$\mu_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k^0+1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G_{k^0}=z_{k^0}\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ its cdf. Let~$z'_{k^0}:=T^{(k^0)}(z'_{k^0})$ and denote~$\mu_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k^0+1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G_{k^0}=z'_{k^0}\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ its cdf. Note that~$x<z_{k^0}\leq z'_{k^0}=T^{(k^0)}(z_{k^0})\leq 1$. Again, we would like to prove that~$\mathds{F}_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}\geq \mathds{F}_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ which implies that the transport map~$T^{(k^0+1)}:=\big(\mathds{F}_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}\big)^{-1}\circ \mathds{F}_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}$ satisfies~$T^{(k^0+1)}(u)\geq u$ for all~$u\in(0,1)$.
 
 Recall that the conditional density~$\mathbf{p}$ of~$G|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}\}$ is given by~\eqref{eq:density} and recall that~$k^0\in I_0$. Observe that~$\mu^0_{k^0}=0$, so that the conditional density of~$G|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G_{k^0}=\mathbf{z}\}$ is
 \begin{align}
 \mathrm{(const)}\,\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}\mathds 1_{g_{k^0}=\mathbf{z}}&\prod_{k< k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big] \\&\times \prod_{k> k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,\mathbf{z}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0\leq k}\!\!g_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,.\notag
 \end{align}
 Set~$\tau:=z'_{k^0}/z_{k^0}\geq 1$ and~$G'_{k^0+1}=\tau G_{k^0+1}$ so that 
 \[
 z_{k^0} G_{k^0+1}=z'_{k^0}G'_{k^0+1}\,.
 \]
 Denote~$G':=(G_1,\ldots,G_{k^0-1},G'_{k^0+1},G_{k^0+2},\ldots,G_K)\in(0,1)^{k^0-1}\times(0,\tau)\times(0,1)^{K-k^0-1}$ and note that the conditional density of~$G'|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G_{k^0}=\tau \mathbf{z}\}$ is
 \begin{align*}
 \mathrm{(const)}\,\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^{k^0-1}\times(0,\tau)\times(0,1)^{K-k^0-1}}
 &\prod_{k< k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]
 \\&\times \prod_{k> k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,\mathbf{z}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0\leq k}\!\!g_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,,
 \end{align*}
 which, up to some normalising constant, is the same as~\eqref{yoyoz1} up to the following change of support
 \[
 \mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}\leftrightarrow \mathds 1_{g'\in(0,1)^{k^0-1}\times(0,\tau)\times(0,1)^{K-k^0-1}}\,.
 \]
 By an abuse of notation, we denote by~$\mathbf{p}$ this function, namely
 \begin{align*}
\mathbf{p}(g)=
 &\prod_{k< k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]
 \\&\times \prod_{k> k^0}g_k^{K-k}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,\mathbf{z}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0\leq k}\!\!g_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,.
 \end{align*}
We deduce that
\begin{align}
 \mathds{F}_{z_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}(t)\geq \mathds{F}_{z'_{k^0}}^{(k^0+1)}(t)\quad
 &\Leftrightarrow\quad \overline{\mathds{P}}(G_{k^0+1}\leq t|G_{k^0}=z_{k^0})\geq
 \overline{\mathds{P}}(G_{k^0+1}\leq t|G_{k^0}=z'_{k^0})\notag\\
 &\Leftrightarrow\quad \overline{\mathds{P}}(G_{k^0+1}\leq t|G_{k^0}=z_{k^0})\geq
 \overline{\mathds{P}}(G'_{k^0+1}\leq \tau t|G_{k^0}=\tau z_{k^0})\notag\\
 &\Leftrightarrow\quad \frac{\int_{\mathcal{D}(t)}\mathbf{p}}{\int_{\mathcal{D}(1)}\mathbf{p}} \geq \frac{\int_{\mathcal{D}(\tau t)}\mathbf{p}}{\int_{\mathcal{D}(\tau)}\mathbf{p}}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow\quad \int_{\mathcal{D}(t)\times\mathcal{D}(\tau) }\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}\geq\int_{\mathcal{D}(\tau t)\times \mathcal{D}(1)}\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}\,, \end{align}
where
\[
 \mathcal{D}(s):=\Big\{(g_1,\ldots,g_{k^0-1},g_{k^0+1}\ldots,g_K)\in(0,1)^{K-1}\ :\ 0< g_{k^0+1}\leq s\Big\}\,.
\]
\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width=0.4\textwidth]{y2}
\caption{The two boxed rectangles have Lebesgue measure, namely~$\tau t$. The~$\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}$  measure of the grey box is greater than the~$\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}$ measure of the white box. } \end{figure}

We now present an inequality on the  to conclude. Observe that we are integrating on domains depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:yoyo2}. The two boxes have same area for the uniform measure and we would like to compare their respective measure for the~$\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}$ measure. We start by the next lemma whose proof is omitted. 
\begin{lemma} Let~$a,b\geq0$. The function 
\[
z\mapsto\cosh(a\, z+b)\times \cosh(a / z+b)
\]
is non-decreasing on the domain~$[1,\infty)$.
\end{lemma}

\noindent
Now, let~$(g_1,\ldots,g_{k^0-1},g_{k^0+2}\ldots,g_K)\in(0,1)^{K-1}$ be fixed in the integrals~\eqref{eq:yoyo123}. We are the looking at the weights of the domains~$(h_1,h_2)\in(0,t)\times (0,\tau)$ and~$(h_3,h_4)\in(0,\tau t)\times (0,1)$ for the weight function~$w$ given by
\begin{align*}
w(h_1,h_2)=&\mathrm{C}_1h_1^{K-k^0-1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell <k^0}\!\!g_\ell\times h_1+F_{K+1})\big]\\
&\times \prod_{k> k^0+1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0,k^0+1\leq k}\!\!g_\ell\times h_1+F_{K+1})\big]\\
&\times h_2^{K-k^0-1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell <k^0}\!\!g_\ell\times h_2+F_{K+1})\big]\\
&\times \prod_{k> k^0+1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0,k^0+1\leq k}\!\!g_\ell\times h_2+F_{K+1})\big]\,,
 \end{align*}
 where the constant~$\mathrm{C}_1$ depends on~$(g_1,\ldots,g_{k^0-1},g_{k^0+2}\ldots,g_K)\in(0,1)^{K-1}$. By the change of variables~$h'_1=h_3/t$ and~$h'_2=t h_4$, the right hand term of~\eqref{eq:yoyo123} is given by the integration on the domain~$(h'_1,h'_2)\in(0,t)\times (0,\tau)$ of the weight function~$w'$ given by
\begin{align*}
w'(h_1',h_2')=
 &\mathrm{C}_1{h'_1}^{K-k^0-1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell <k^0}\!\!g_\ell\times t\times h'_1+F_{K+1})\big]\\
&\times \prod_{k> k^0+1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0,k^0+1\leq k}\!\!g_\ell\times t\times h'_1+F_{K+1})\big]\\
 &\times {h'_2}^{K-k^0-1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell <k^0}\!\!g_\ell\times h'_2/t+F_{K+1})\big]\\
&\times \prod_{k> k^0+1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell\neq k^0,k^0+1\leq k}\!\!g_\ell\times h'_2/t+F_{K+1})\big]\,.
 \end{align*}
Now, invoke Lemma~\ref{lem:coshyoyo} with 
\begin{align*}
a&={\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}(1-F_{K+1})\,\,z_{k^0}\!\!\prod_{1\leq \ell <k^0}\!\!g_\ell\times  h\\
b&={\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}F_{K+1}\\
z&=t\geq 1\,,
\end{align*}
where~$h=h_1$ or~$h_2$, to get that~$w'\geq w$ and so 
\[
\int_{\mathcal{D}(t)\times\mathcal{D}(\tau) }\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}\geq\int_{\mathcal{D}(\tau t)\times \mathcal{D}(1)}\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{p}\,,
\]
which concludes this part of the proof.


 \medskip
 
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \it Step 3.3: } We continue by induction with the other transport maps in Knothe-Rosenblatt's construction. Assume that we have built~$z':=(z'_{k},\ldots,z'_{k^0})$ and~$z:=(z_{k},\ldots,z_{k^0})$ for some~$k>k^0$. Denote~$\mu_{z}^{(k+1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z}^{(k+1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k+1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, \underbrace{G_{k}=z_{k},\ldots, G_{k^0}=z_{k^0}}_{\mathrm{denoted\ }G^{[k,k^0]}=z}\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z}^{(k+1)}$ its cdf. Denote~$\mu_{z'}^{(k+1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z'}^{(k+1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k+1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, \underbrace{G_{k}=z'_{k},\ldots, G_{k^0}=z'_{k^0}}_{G^{[k,k^0]}=z'}\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k+1)}$ its cdf. Note that~$z\leq z'=T^{(k)}(z)\leq 1$. Again, we would prove that~$\mathds{F}_{z}^{(k+1)}\geq \mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k+1)}$ which implies that the transport map~$T^{(k+1)}:=\big(\mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k+1)}\big)^{-1}\circ \mathds{F}_{z}^{(k+1)}$ satisfies~$T^{(k+1)}(u)\geq u$ for all~$u\in(0,1)$.
 
 For~$\mathbf{z}\in(0,1)^{k-k^0}\times(x,1)$, the conditional density of~$G|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G^{[k,k^0]}=\mathbf{z}\}$ is
 \begin{align}
 \mathrm{(const)}\,\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}&\mathds 1_{g^{[k,k^0]}=\mathbf{z}}
 \prod_{m< k^0}g_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^mg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\notag]\\
 &\times \prod_{k^0\leq m\leq k}\mathbf{z}_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{1\leq \ell<k^0}\!\!g_\ell\,\,\prod_{n=k^0}^m\mathbf{z}_n+F_{K+1})\big]\notag\\
&\times \prod_{k<m}g_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{1\leq \ell<k^0}\!\!g_\ell\,\,\prod_{n=k^0}^k\mathbf{z}_n\prod_{k< \ell\leq m}\!\!g_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,.\notag
 \end{align}
Set~$\tau:=\prod_{n=k^0}^kz'_n/\prod_{n=k^0}^kz_n\geq 1$ and~$G'_{k}=\tau G_{k^0+1}$ so that 
 \[
\Big[\prod_{n=k^0}^kz'_n\Big] G_{k+1}=\Big[\prod_{n=k^0}^kz_n\Big] G'_{k+1}\,.
 \]
Then the proof follows the same idea as in {\it Step 3.2} and we will not detail it here.
 \medskip
 
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \it Step 3.4: } This is the last step of the proof. Assume that we have built~$z':=(z'_{K},\ldots,z'_{k^0})$ and~$z:=(z_{K},\ldots,z_{k^0})$. Denote~$\mu_{z}^{(k^0-1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z}^{(k^0-1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k^0-1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G^{[K,k^0]}=z\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z}^{(k^0-1)}$ its cdf. Denote~$\mu_{z'}^{(k^0-1)}$ the following conditional law  
 \[
 \mu_{z'}^{(k^0-1)}:=\mathrm{law}\big[G_{k^0-1}|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G^{[K,k^0]}=z'\}\big]\,,
 \]
 and~$\mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k^01)}$ its cdf. Note that~$z\leq z'=T^{(K)}(z)\leq 1$. Again, we would prove that~$\mathds{F}_{z}^{(k^0-1)}\geq \mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k^0-1)}$ which implies that the transport map~$T^{(k^0-1)}:=\big(\mathds{F}_{z'}^{(k^0-1)}\big)^{-1}\circ \mathds{F}_{z}^{(k^0-1)}$ satisfies~$T^{(k^0-1)}(u)\geq u$ for all~$u\in(0,1)$.

For~$\mathbf{z}\in(0,1)^{K-k^0}\times(x,1)$, the conditional density of~$G|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}, G^{[K,k^0]}=\mathbf{z}\}$ is
 \begin{align}
 \mathrm{(const)}\,\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}&\mathds 1_{g^{[K,k^0]}=\mathbf{z}}
 \prod_{m< k^0}g_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^mg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\notag\\
 &\times \prod_{k^0\leq m\leq K}\mathbf{z}_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{1\leq \ell<k^0}\!\!g_\ell\,\,\prod_{n=k^0}^m\mathbf{z}_n+F_{K+1})\big]\,.\notag
 \end{align}

\noindent
Now, let~$(g_1,\ldots,g_{k^0-2})\in(0,1)^{k^0-2}$ be fixed and denote by
 \begin{align}
\forall g\in(0,1),\quad
w_{z}(g):=&g^{K-k^0+1}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_{k^0-1}}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^{k^0-2}g_\ell\times g+F_{K+1})\big]\notag\\
 &\times \prod_{k^0\leq m\leq K}\mathbf{z}_m^{K-m}\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_m}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{n=k^0}^m\mathbf{z}_n\prod_{\ell=1}^{k^0-2}g_\ell\times g+F_{K+1})\big]\,.\notag
 \end{align}
 and, substituting~$z$ by~$z'$, define~$w_{z'}$ as well. Let~$t\in(0,1)$. Following the idea of  {\it Step 3.2}, one can check that it is sufficient to prove that
 \[
 \int_0^t\Big(\int_0^1w_{z}(g)w_{z'}(g')\mathrm dg'\Big)\mathrm dg
 \geq
  \int_0^1\Big(\int_0^tw_{z}(g)w_{z'}(g')\mathrm dg'\Big)\mathrm dg\,.
 \]
 Substituting 
 \[
  \int_0^t\Big(\int_0^tw_{z}(g)w_{z'}(g')\mathrm dg'\Big)\mathrm dg
 \]
 on both parts, one is reduced to prove that
  \[
 \int_0^t\Big(\int_t^1w_{z}(g)w_{z'}(g')\mathrm dg'\Big)\mathrm dg
 \geq
\int_0^t\Big(\int_t^1w_{z'}(g)w_{z}(g')\mathrm dg'\Big)\mathrm dg\,.
 \]
 Observe that~$g\leq g'$ in the last two integrals. Now, we have this lemma whose proof is omitted. 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$0<a\leq a'$ and~$b>0$. The function 
\[
z\mapsto\frac{\cosh(a\, z+b)}{\cosh(a'z+b)}
\]
is non-increasing on the domain~$(0,\infty)$.
\end{lemma}

\noindent
Let~$g\leq g'$. From Lemma~\ref{lem:coshyoyo2}, we deduce that~$\cosh(a g+b)\cosh(a' g'+b)\geq \cosh(a g'+b)\cosh(a' g+b)$, proving that~$w_{z}(g)w_{z'}(g')\geq w_{z'}(g)w_{z}(g')$. It proves that~$T^{(k^0-1)}(u)\geq u$ for all~$u\in(0,1)$.

We then proceed by induction for~$k^0-1\to k^0-2\to\cdots\to 1$. The proof follows the same line as above, {\it Step 3.4}.

nodes.name: WPRDS reduction
nodes.statement_short: Reduce FDR control to the WPRDS property.
nodes.statement:
We rely on the {\bf Weak Positive Regression Dependency (WPRDS) property} to prove the result, one may consult~\cite[Page 173]{giraud2014introduction} for instance. We say that a function~$g:[0,1]^K\to \mathds{R}^+$ is {\it nondecreasing} if for any~$p,q\in[0,1]^K$ such that~$p_k\geq q_k$ for every~$k=1,\ldots, K$, we have~$g(p)\geq g(q)$. We say that a Borel set~$\Gamma\in[0,1]^K$ is {\it nondecreasing} if~$g=\mathds 1_\Gamma$ is nondecreasing. In other words  if~$y \in \gamma$ and if~$z\geq0$, then~$y+z \in \gamma$. We say that the~$p$-values~$(\,\widehat p_1=\widehat\alpha_{0,1,K+1},\ldots,\widehat p_K=\widehat\alpha_{K-1,K,K+1})$ satisfy the WPRDS property if for any nondecreasing set~$\Gamma$ 
 and for all~$k^0\in I_0$, the function 
\[
u\mapsto \mathds{P}_{\mu^0}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
\]
where~$\mu^0=\beta^0$ in our  orthogonal design case, and we recall that
\[
I_0=\big\{k\in[K]\ :\ \mathds H_{0,k}\text{ is true}\big\}\,.
\] 
To prove Theorem \ref{thm:independentTest}, note that it is sufficient~\cite[Chapter~8]{giraud2014introduction} to prove that 
\begin{equation} u\mapsto \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
\end{equation}
where~$\overline{\mathds{E}},\overline{\operatorname{\mathds{P}}}$ will denote that expectations and probabilities are conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$ and under the hypothesis that~$\mu^0=X^\top X\beta^0$. Note that one can integrate in~$\lambda_{K+1}$ to get the statement of Theorem \ref{thm:independentTest}.

nodes.statement_short: BH controls FDR under WPRDS.
nodes.statement: We rely on the {\bf Weak Positive Regression Dependency (WPRDS) property} to prove the result, one may consult~\cite[Page 173]{giraud2014introduction} for instance.

nodes.statement_short: Define nondecreasing functions/sets and WPRDS.
nodes.statement:

We say that a Borel set~$\Gamma\in[0,1]^K$ is {\it nondecreasing} if~$g=\mathds 1_\Gamma$ is nondecreasing. In other words  if~$y \in \gamma$ and if~$z\geq0$, then~$y+z \in \gamma$. We say that the~$p$-values~$(\,\widehat p_1=\widehat\alpha_{0,1,K+1},\ldots,\widehat p_K=\widehat\alpha_{K-1,K,K+1})$ satisfy the WPRDS property if for any nondecreasing set~$\Gamma$ 
 and for all~$k^0\in I_0$, the function 
\[
u\mapsto \mathds{P}_{\mu^0}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
\]

\]

nodes.name: Sufficient condition
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to prove monotonicity conditionally on the entering sequence and $\lambda_{K+1}$.

nodes.name: Equation (7.11)
nodes.statement: u\mapsto \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]\text{ is nondecreasing}
nodes.label: yoyonondecresaing

nodes.name: Step 1
nodes.statement_short: Joint law and change of variables to $G$.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 1: }We start by giving the joint law of the LARS knots under the alternative in the orthogonal design case. Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} and~\eqref{zazcosh} show that, conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,\lambda_{K+1}\}$,~$(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K)$ is distributed on the set~$\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \cdots\geq \lambda_K\geq \lambda_{K+1}$ and it has a coordinate-wise nondecreasing density. 
 
 Now we can assume without loss of generality  that~$\sigma^2 =1$, in addition because of orthogonality 
~$\rho_k^2=1$ implying that~$F_k=\Phi(\lambda_k)$~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}=\Phi_i\circ\Phi_j^{-1}=\mathrm{Id}$.  We deduce that, conditional on~$\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots, \overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}\}$,~$(F_1,\ldots,F_K)$ is distributed on the set
\[
\big\{
(f_1,\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^K\ :\ 
1\geq f_1\geq f_2\geq \cdots\geq f_K\geq F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\]
it has an {\bf explicit density} given by~\eqref{zazcosh}, and we denote it by~$h_{\mu^0}$. By the change of variables~$G_k:=\frac{ F_k-F_{K+1}}{ F_{k-1}-F_{K+1}}$ one  obtains that the distribution of~$(G_1,\ldots,G_K)$ is supported on~$[0,1]^K$. More precisely, define
\begin{align*}
\psi(f_1,\ldots,f_K)& :=(g_1,\ldots,g_K)   := (\frac{ f_1-F_{K+1}}{1-F_{K+1}},\ldots,\frac{ f_K-F_{K+1}}{f_{K-1}-F_{K+1}}) \\
\psi^{-1}(g_1,\ldots,g_K)&:=\Big((1-F_{K+1})g_1+F_{K+1},\ldots,(1-F_{K+1})g_1g_2\ldots g_K+F_{K+1}\Big),
\end{align*}
whose inverse Jacobian determinant is 
\[
\det\Big[\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial f_1} \cdots\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial f_K}\Big]^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^K(f_{k-1}-F_{K+1})=(1-F_{K+1})^K\prod_{k=1}^{K}g_k^{K-k}\,.
\] 
We deduce that the density  of~$(G_1,\ldots,G_K)|\{\overline \imath_1,\ldots,\overline \imath_K,F_{K+1}\}$  at point~$g$ with respect to Lebesgue measure is 
\begin{align} \mathbf{p}(g):=
\mathrm{(const)}\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}g_k^{K-k}&\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,,
\end{align}
where we have used~\eqref{zazcosh}. From~\eqref{zaza5} and~\eqref{eq:BetaF}, one has 
\begin{equation} \widehat p_k =1-\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)} \bigg( \frac{ F_k-F_{K+1}}{ F_{k-1}-F_{K+1}} \bigg)
=1-\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)}(G_k)
\end{equation}
 where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference. We deduce that for any~$v\in(0,1)$ and for any~$\ell\in[K]$, 
\begin{align*}













\widehat p_k &= v
\Leftrightarrow
(G_1,\ldots,G_K)\in 
{[0,1]^K\cap\{\boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-k+1)}^{-1}(1-v)= G_k\}
}

\,,
\end{align*}
so that 
\begin{equation} \overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(\,\widehat p_1,\ldots,\widehat p_K)\in\Gamma\big|\widehat p_{k^0}\leq u\big]=\overline{\mathds{P}}\big[(G_1,\ldots,G_K)\in\overline\Gamma\big|G_{k^0}\geq \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta(1,K-\ell+1)}^{-1}(1-u)\big]\,,
\end{equation}
where~$\overline\Gamma$ can be proved to be a {\bf nonincreasing Borel set} from~\eqref{eq:yoyoFDR}.

\mathrm{(const)}\mathds 1_{g\in(0,1)^K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}g_k^{K-k}&\cosh\big[{\mu^0_{\overline\imath_k}}((1-F_{K+1})\prod_{\ell=1}^kg_\ell+F_{K+1})\big]\,,

nodes.name: p-values via G
